lessons.title: Scene safety and calling for help
lessons.when: Before you touch anyone at any emergency: make it safe, get help coming, and ask permission.
recognize: Traffic, fire, smoke, gas smell or fallen power lines
Deep, fast or rough water, or slippery rocks
An angry person, animal or a crowd
Blood or body fluids you could touch
More than one injured person
A person who is unresponsive or clearly badly hurt
steps: Stop and look around before you go in. If it is not safe, stay back and call.
Make it safer if you can: switch off engines, set up hazard lights, turn off power.
Put on gloves if you have them, or use a plastic bag over your hand.
Say who you are and ask: "Can I help you?" If they say no, respect it and call.
If they are unresponsive, you may help: act as a reasonable person would want.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) or point at one person and tell them to call.
Put the phone on speaker and stay with the person while you talk.
Say where you are, what happened, how many are hurt, and whether they are awake and breathing.
Do not hang up until the call taker tells you to. Send someone to meet the ambulance.
dont: Do not become a second casualty: never enter fire, traffic, live wires or rough water to rescue.
Do not assume someone else has already called.
Do not shout "someone call" to a crowd; pick one person and give a clear job.
Do not move an injured person unless they are in danger where they lie.
Do not leave the person alone if you can avoid it.
lessons.call: Call at once for anyone unresponsive, not breathing normally, bleeding heavily, with chest pain, stroke signs, severe allergy or a serious injury. If unsure, call: the call taker will help you decide.
special: For a child, ask a parent or carer for consent if one is present; if not, help.
In remote areas or where ambulances are slow, also ask the call taker or locals about the fastest way to the nearest hospital.
Save the local emergency number and your accommodation address in your phone when you arrive somewhere new.
lessons.why: Most rescuers who get hurt rushed in without looking. A few seconds to check for traffic, power, fire or water keeps you able to help, and an injured rescuer doubles the problem. Gloves or a barrier protect you both from infections carried in blood. Asking for consent respects the person; an unresponsive person cannot answer, so the law in most places assumes they would want help. Calling early matters more than almost anything else, because ambulances take time and the call taker can coach you through CPR and other steps. A speaker phone keeps your hands free. Giving a clear location first means help can still find you if the call drops.

quiz.q: A motorbike has crashed on a busy road at night. The rider lies still in the lane. What do you do first?
options: Run to the rider and check breathing
Check for traffic, warn or stop vehicles safely, then approach
Drag the rider to the roadside immediately
quiz.why: Your safety comes first. Make the scene safer, for example with hazard lights and people warning traffic, before you approach.

quiz.q: A crowd has gathered around a collapsed man. Several people are filming. How do you make sure help is called?
options: Point at one person: "You in the blue shirt, call 911 and come back to me."
Wait until you have checked him fully before calling
quiz.why: Giving one named person a clear job avoids everyone thinking someone else did it. Asking them to come back confirms the call was made.

quiz.q: On the phone, what should you say first?
options: How the accident happened in detail
quiz.why: Location comes first so help can be sent even if the call drops. Then say what happened and the person's condition.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: The first 60 seconds
lessons.when: You reach someone who has collapsed or been hurt and need to decide quickly what to do.
recognize: Person collapsed, lying still or not reacting
Not breathing, or only gasping or making odd noises
Heavy bleeding, spurting or pooling blood
Pale, grey, sweaty or blue skin
Confused, very drowsy or hard to wake
steps: Danger: check it is safe for you, them and bystanders.
Response: tap their shoulders and shout "Are you OK? Open your eyes!"
No response: shout for help, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) on speaker, and ask for an AED.
Airway: turn them onto their back, tilt the head back and lift the chin.
Breathing: look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
Not breathing normally or only gasping: start CPR now and send someone for an AED.
Breathing normally: check quickly for heavy bleeding and press hard on it, then use the recovery position.
Awake and talking: ask what happened, what hurts, and look for bleeding, allergies, chest pain or stroke signs.
Keep checking breathing and response until help takes over. If breathing stops, start CPR.
dont: Do not spend more than 10 seconds checking breathing.
Do not mistake gasping or snoring breaths for normal breathing: treat it as not breathing.
Do not look for a pulse; laypeople are not reliable at it and it wastes time.
Do not give food, drink or medicine to someone who is drowsy or unresponsive.
lessons.call: Call immediately if they do not respond, are not breathing normally, have heavy bleeding, or have chest pain, stroke signs, severe allergy or trouble breathing.
special: Child or infant who is not breathing: ERC advises 5 rescue breaths first, then CPR; see the child and infant CPR lessons.
If you are alone with no phone and a child or drowning victim is not breathing, give about 1 minute of CPR before going for help.
Possible neck injury: open the airway with as little head movement as possible, but breathing always comes first.
lessons.why: The order Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation puts the biggest killers first. An unresponsive person's tongue can fall back and block the throat, so tilting the head and lifting the chin opens the airway. Normal breathing tells you the heart is pumping; without it, the brain starts to die within minutes, so CPR must begin straight away. Gasping is common in the first minutes after the heart stops and is easily mistaken for breathing, which is why it counts as not breathing. Heavy bleeding can kill in a few minutes too, so firm pressure comes early. Calling at the start means professional help and an AED arrive sooner.

quiz.q: A woman collapses at a market. She does not respond, and every few seconds she makes a deep snoring gasp. What do you do?
options: Put her in the recovery position, she is breathing
Wait a minute to see if the breathing improves
quiz.why: Occasional gasps are not normal breathing. They often happen right after the heart stops, so call and start CPR.

quiz.q: How long should you check for normal breathing?
quiz.why: Look, listen and feel for no more than 10 seconds. If you are not sure it is normal, start CPR.

quiz.q: A man is unresponsive but breathing normally after falling off a ladder. His thigh is bleeding heavily. What comes first?
options: Press hard on the bleeding wound and call 911
quiz.why: He is breathing, so the next threat is blood loss. Press firmly on the wound and make sure help is called.

sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025
AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Recovery position
lessons.when: Someone is unresponsive but breathing normally and you need to keep their airway open.
recognize: Does not respond when you tap and shout
Breathing normally (regular, not gasping)
May be drowsy after a seizure, faint, drinking or drugs
May vomit or gurgle
steps: Kneel beside them. Remove glasses and bulky items from pockets.
Put the arm nearest you out at a right angle, elbow bent, palm up.
Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of that hand against their near cheek.
With your other hand, pull the far knee up so the foot is flat on the ground.
Pull on the bent knee to roll them towards you onto their side.
Bend the top leg so hip and knee are at right angles, to stop them rolling.
Tilt the head back slightly so the airway stays open and the mouth points down.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if not done. Check breathing every minute.
If breathing stops or becomes gasping, roll them onto their back and start CPR.
dont: Do not leave them on their back if they are unresponsive and might vomit.
Do not put anything in their mouth or give them a drink.
Do not stop checking breathing; it can change quickly.
Do not use the recovery position if they are not breathing normally: start CPR instead.
lessons.call: Call emergency services for anyone who stays unresponsive, even if they are breathing. Call again or tell the call taker if breathing changes.
special: Infant: hold them in your arms, face down along your forearm with the head lower than the body, and watch breathing.
Pregnant (late pregnancy): put her on her left side to take pressure off the large blood vessels.
Possible spinal injury: if they are breathing and the airway is clear, leave them as found; roll them only if the airway is at risk or you must leave them.
lessons.why: When someone is unresponsive, their muscles relax. On their back, the tongue can fall back and block the throat, and vomit or blood can run into the lungs. Lying on their side with the head tilted lets fluids drain out of the mouth and keeps the tongue forward. The bent top leg and the hand under the cheek make the position stable, so you can step away briefly to get help. Breathing can fade without warning, which is why you keep checking every minute. If they stay in the position for a long time, turning them to the other side after about 30 minutes eases pressure on the lower arm.

timer.label: Turn to the other side (keep checking breathing every minute)

quiz.q: Your friend drank too much and is now unresponsive on the beach but breathing normally. What should you do?
options: Leave him on his back to sleep it off
Put him in the recovery position, call 911 and keep checking breathing
Sit him upright against a tree
Splash cold water on his face and give coffee
quiz.why: On his side his airway stays open and vomit can drain out. An unresponsive person needs emergency help.

quiz.q: While in the recovery position, the person's breathing turns into occasional gasps. What next?
options: Keep them on their side and wait
Roll them onto their back and start CPR
quiz.why: Gasping is not normal breathing. Roll them back and start CPR, and send for an AED.

quiz.q: Which way should the mouth face in the recovery position?
quiz.why: With the mouth pointing down, vomit, blood or saliva can drain out instead of into the lungs.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: CPR for adults
lessons.when: An adult (or teenager) is unresponsive and not breathing normally, or only gasping.
recognize: Does not respond to tapping and shouting
Not breathing, or only occasional gasps
May have collapsed suddenly
Skin may be grey or blue
A brief jerking like a seizure can happen as the heart stops
steps: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) on speaker and send someone for an AED.
Kneel beside them on a firm surface. Put the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest.
Place your other hand on top, lock your elbows, and get your shoulders straight over your hands.
Push hard, 5 to 6 cm deep, and fast, 100 to 120 times a minute.
Let the chest come fully back up after every push. Keep pauses as short as possible.
If untrained or unwilling to give breaths, keep pushing nonstop: hands-only CPR still saves lives.
If trained and willing: after 30 pushes, tilt the head, lift the chin, pinch the nose, give 2 breaths.
Each breath lasts about 1 second and should make the chest rise. Then go straight back to 30 pushes.
Turn on the AED as soon as it arrives. Swap rescuers every 2 minutes. Continue until help takes over.
dont: Do not wait to see if they start breathing: start CPR at once.
Do not push too gently or too slowly; aim for the beat of "Stayin' Alive".
Do not lean on the chest between pushes; let it rise fully.
Do not stop for more than 10 seconds, for example for breaths or to check them.
Do not fear hurting them: broken ribs can happen and are far less serious than death.
lessons.call: Always call emergency services before or as you start CPR. If alone with a phone, put it on speaker so you can keep pushing.
special: Pregnant (visibly): do CPR as normal; if someone can help, have them push the bump gently to her left side.
Elderly: same depth and rate; do not hold back for fear of injury.
Suspected opioid overdose: give naloxone if available, but do not delay CPR for it.
lessons.why: When the heart stops, blood stops reaching the brain, and brain damage starts within a few minutes. Pushing hard on the chest squeezes the heart and pumps some blood to the brain and heart muscle. Depth and speed matter: too shallow or too slow moves little blood, and letting the chest rise fully lets the heart refill. Every pause lets the pressure drop, so keep breaks short. In the first minutes there is still oxygen in the blood, which is why hands-only CPR works well for adults. Rescue breaths add oxygen and help more as time goes on. CPR rarely restarts the heart alone; it buys time until the AED can shock it.

quiz.q: You are alone with a man who collapsed and is not breathing. You have your phone. What do you do?
options: Run to find help, then come back
Call 911 on speaker and start chest compressions
quiz.why: Call on speaker so you can keep your hands on the chest. Start compressions right away and ask the call taker about an AED.

quiz.q: How deep and how fast should you push on an adult's chest?
options: As deep as possible, 80 per minute
quiz.why: 5 to 6 cm at 100 to 120 per minute moves blood well without excessive force.

quiz.q: You have never been trained and do not want to give mouth-to-mouth to a stranger. What is best?
options: Do nothing until the ambulance comes
quiz.why: Hands-only CPR for an adult is far better than no CPR. Keep going until help or an AED arrives.

sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025

lessons.title: CPR for children
lessons.when: A child from 1 year old to puberty is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
recognize: Does not respond when you tap and shout
Not breathing, or only occasional gasps
Floppy, pale, grey or blue lips
Often follows choking, drowning, illness or injury
steps: Shout for help. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) on speaker and ask for an AED.
Tilt the head back gently, lift the chin, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs.
Give 5 rescue breaths, each about 1 second, enough to make the chest rise (ERC advice).
Put the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone; use two hands for a big child.
Push down one third of the chest depth, about 5 cm, at 100 to 120 a minute.
Let the chest come fully back up after each push.
Give 30 compressions, then 2 breaths. Repeat without long pauses.
Use the AED as soon as it arrives, with child pads if available. Follow its voice.
Keep going until help takes over or the child starts breathing normally.
dont: Do not skip breaths if you can give them: children usually need oxygen most.
Do not blow too hard; just enough to see the chest rise.
Do not leave to call before giving CPR if you can call on speaker instead.
Do not do nothing because you are unsure: hands-only CPR is better than no CPR.
lessons.call: Call at once, using a speaker phone. If you are alone with no phone, give CPR for about 1 minute before going for help, carrying a small child with you if you can.
special: AHA starts with compressions (30:2) and ERC starts with 5 breaths; both work. Starting quickly matters most.
Two trained rescuers may use 15 compressions to 2 breaths; one rescuer uses 30:2.
A teenager who looks like an adult: use adult CPR.
lessons.why: Children's hearts are usually healthy. Their hearts most often stop because of a lack of oxygen, from choking, drowning or severe illness. That is why breaths matter more for children than for adults, and why European guidance starts with 5 rescue breaths. Compressions then pump that oxygen to the brain. Pushing one third of the chest depth, about 5 cm, is deep enough to move blood without needing adult force; one hand is enough for most children. Letting the chest rise fully lets the heart refill between pushes. An AED can still help a child, and child pads lower the shock to a safer level.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old is pulled from a pool, unresponsive and not breathing. A friend is calling 911. What do you do first (ERC)?
options: Give 5 rescue breaths, then start CPR
Turn her upside down to drain water
Put her in the recovery position
quiz.why: Children and drowning victims usually lack oxygen, so 5 rescue breaths come first, then 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

quiz.q: How deep should compressions be for a child?
options: About one third of the chest depth, about 5 cm
As deep as for a large adult, 6 to 7 cm
quiz.why: About one third of the chest depth, around 5 cm, moves enough blood in a child.

quiz.q: You are alone in a remote house with no phone signal, and your child is not breathing. What should you do?
options: Give about 1 minute of CPR, then go for help, taking the child if possible
Wait for the child to wake up
quiz.why: A short period of CPR first gives oxygen to the brain. Then you must get help, ideally carrying a small child with you.

sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025

lessons.title: CPR for infants
lessons.when: A baby under 1 year old is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
recognize: Does not respond when you tap the foot and speak loudly
Not breathing, or only occasional gasps
Floppy, pale, grey or blue around the lips
May follow choking, drowning or illness
steps: Shout for help. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) on speaker.
Lay the baby on their back on a firm surface. Keep the head level, not tilted far back.
Seal your mouth over the baby's mouth and nose. Give 5 gentle breaths that make the chest rise (ERC).
Wrap both hands around the chest and put both thumbs side by side on the lower half of the breastbone.
If you cannot encircle the chest, use the heel of one hand on the same spot.
Push down one third of the chest depth, about 4 cm, at 100 to 120 a minute.
Let the chest fully rise after each push.
Give 30 compressions, then 2 gentle breaths. Repeat without long pauses.
Continue until help takes over or the baby starts breathing normally.
dont: Do not tilt a baby's head far back; a level, neutral position keeps the airway open.
Do not blow big breaths; small puffs from your cheeks are enough to lift the chest.
Do not shake the baby to wake them.
Do not stop CPR to check for signs of life unless the baby moves, cries or breathes normally.
lessons.call: Call at once using a speaker phone. If you are alone with no phone, give CPR for about 1 minute, then carry the baby with you to get help.
special: AHA starts with compressions and ERC starts with 5 breaths; either way, start fast and include breaths.
Two trained rescuers may use 15 compressions to 2 breaths, with the two-thumb technique.
An AED can be used on a baby; use child pads or a child setting if available, placed front and back.
lessons.why: Babies' hearts almost always stop because of a lack of oxygen, from choking, breathing problems or drowning, not a heart problem. So breaths are essential. A baby's head is large and the airway is soft and easily kinked, which is why a level head position works better than tilting far back. Covering the mouth and nose together lets you deliver small breaths. The two-thumb technique wraps the chest and gives deeper, steadier compressions than fingers alone; the heel of one hand is an alternative if your hands cannot encircle the chest. One third of the chest depth, about 4 cm, is enough to pump blood without needing force.

quiz.q: A 6-month-old is limp and not breathing in her cot. How do you open her airway?
options: Tilt the head back as far as possible
Keep the head level (neutral) and lift the chin
Put a pillow under her head
quiz.why: A baby's airway kinks if the head is tilted too far. A level position with the chin lifted keeps it open.

quiz.q: How deep should compressions be for an infant?
options: About 4 cm, one third of the chest depth
Just enough to dent the skin
quiz.why: About one third of the chest depth, around 4 cm, is right for an infant.

quiz.q: Where do your mouth and the baby's face meet for rescue breaths?
options: Your mouth over the baby's mouth only
Your mouth over the baby's mouth and nose
Your mouth over the nose only
quiz.why: A baby's face is small, so covering mouth and nose together gives a good seal for gentle breaths.

sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025

lessons.title: Using an AED
lessons.when: Someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, and an AED (automated external defibrillator) is available.
recognize: A green or red box marked AED, often with a heart and lightning bolt
Found in airports, malls, hotels, gyms, offices and some resorts
The person is unresponsive and not breathing normally
CPR has started or is needed
steps: Keep CPR going while someone opens the AED and turns it on. Follow its voice.
Bare the chest. Wipe it dry; shave or tear off pads quickly if hair stops them sticking.
Stick one pad below the right collarbone and the other on the left side, below the armpit.
Follow the pictures on the pads. For small children, place pads front and back if they would touch.
When it analyses, stop CPR and make sure nobody touches the person.
If it advises a shock, shout "Stand clear!", check nobody is touching, and press the button.
Restart CPR straight away after the shock, or if no shock is advised.
Leave the pads on and the AED switched on. Follow its prompts until help takes over.
dont: Do not wait for the AED to start CPR; start CPR first and use the AED as soon as it arrives.
Do not touch the person while it analyses or shocks.
Do not put pads over a medicine patch, a pacemaker bump or wet skin; remove patches and dry the chest.
Do not remove the pads or switch it off, even if the person starts to recover.
Do not be afraid: an AED will only shock if it detects a heart rhythm that needs it.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) before or while getting the AED. Ask the call taker where the nearest AED is.
special: Children under 8 years or about 25 kg: use child pads or a child key or setting if available; if not, use adult pads.
Infants: an AED with child settings is preferred, but an adult AED is better than none.
Water: move the person out of puddles or off wet sand if you can and dry the chest; metal or wet ground nearby is safe if nobody touches them during the shock.
lessons.why: Many sudden collapses in adults are caused by a chaotic heart rhythm called ventricular fibrillation, where the heart quivers instead of pumping. CPR keeps some blood moving, but only an electric shock can reset the rhythm. Every minute without a shock lowers the chance of survival, which is why the AED should be used the moment it arrives. The AED is designed for untrained people: it talks you through each step, reads the heart rhythm itself, and will not shock a heart that does not need it. Pads on a dry, bare chest make good contact. Restarting CPR straight after the shock keeps blood flowing while the heart recovers.

quiz.q: The AED arrives while you are doing CPR. What do you do?
options: Keep CPR going while someone turns it on and attaches the pads
Stop CPR and read the manual
Wait for the ambulance to use it
quiz.why: Use the AED as soon as possible, keeping CPR going until it tells you to stop.

quiz.q: The AED has just given a shock. What next?
options: Check for a pulse for 1 minute
Restart CPR immediately and follow the prompts
Put the person in the recovery position
quiz.why: Restart CPR straight away. The AED will tell you when it wants to analyse again.

quiz.q: The person was pulled out of the sea and is soaking wet. Can you use the AED?
options: Yes: move them off wet ground if possible, dry the chest, attach pads
Only after they are completely dry
quiz.why: Wipe the chest dry and avoid anyone touching the person during the shock. Drowning victims need breaths and CPR too.

sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025

lessons.title: Choking (adult and child)
lessons.when: An adult or a child over 1 year old has something stuck in the throat.
recognize: Sudden coughing, gagging or clutching the throat while eating
Cannot speak, cough or breathe (severe)
Weak, silent cough or high-pitched noise when breathing in
Face turning red, then blue or grey
Nods yes when asked "Are you choking?"
steps: Ask "Are you choking?" If they can cough, encourage them to keep coughing hard.
If the cough is weak or they cannot breathe or speak, act now and send someone to call.
Stand beside and slightly behind them. Support the chest and lean them well forward.
Give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If still stuck, stand behind, put a fist just above the navel, grab it with your other hand.
Pull sharply inwards and upwards. Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts.
Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until it comes out or they become unresponsive.
If they become unresponsive, lower them to the ground, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) and start CPR.
Before giving breaths, look in the mouth and remove an object only if you can see it.
dont: Do not slap the back of someone who is coughing well; let them cough.
Do not do blind finger sweeps in the mouth; you can push the object deeper.
Do not give food or water to someone who is choking.
Do not let them go off alone to the toilet; stay with them.
Do not skip a doctor's check after abdominal thrusts.
lessons.call: Call if the cough is weak or they cannot breathe, if they become unresponsive, or if they still have trouble breathing or swallowing afterwards. Anyone given abdominal thrusts should see a doctor.
special: Pregnant or very large person: give chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts, hands on the centre of the chest.
Small child: kneel or sit to reach them; use less force, but the same steps.
Alone and choking: call 911, then thrust your upper belly hard against a chair back or table edge.
lessons.why: A strong cough is the best way to clear the airway, so if they can cough, you help them keep coughing. When the cough fails, back blows use sudden force and gravity, with the person leaning forward, to knock the object loose. Abdominal thrusts push the diaphragm up and force air out of the lungs like a cork from a bottle. Alternating the two works better than either alone. If the person becomes unresponsive, chest compressions also raise pressure in the chest and can push the object out, so CPR is the right next step. Abdominal thrusts can injure organs, which is why a doctor should check them afterwards.

quiz.q: A man at a restaurant is coughing loudly and going red, but he can talk. What should you do?
options: Encourage him to keep coughing and stay with him
quiz.why: A strong cough is clearing the airway. Stay close and be ready to act if it becomes weak.

quiz.q: A woman cannot speak or cough and is clutching her throat. You have given 5 back blows with no success. What next?
options: Sweep your finger in her mouth
Lay her down and start CPR
quiz.why: After 5 back blows, give 5 abdominal thrusts, then keep alternating.

quiz.q: She becomes unresponsive in your arms. What do you do?
options: Keep giving abdominal thrusts standing up
Lower her to the ground, call 911 and start CPR
Put her in the recovery position
Wait for her to wake up
quiz.why: Chest compressions can push the object out and keep blood moving. Check the mouth before giving breaths.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025

lessons.title: Choking (baby under 1)
lessons.when: A baby under 1 year old has something stuck in the throat.
recognize: Sudden coughing, gagging or wheezing, often while feeding or playing with small objects
Cannot cry, cough or breathe
Weak, silent cough or high-pitched noise
Face red, then blue or grey around the lips
Becomes floppy or unresponsive
steps: If the baby is coughing strongly, let them cough and watch closely.
If the cough is silent or they cannot breathe, shout for help and send someone to call.
Lay the baby face down along your forearm, head lower than chest, supporting the jaw with your hand.
Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand.
If still stuck, turn the baby face up along your other forearm, head lower than chest.
Put two fingers, or the heel of one hand, on the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line.
Give up to 5 chest thrusts, sharper and slower than CPR compressions.
Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until it comes out.
If the baby becomes unresponsive, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) and start infant CPR.
dont: Never give abdominal thrusts to a baby; they can damage the liver and other organs.
Do not do blind finger sweeps; remove an object only if you can clearly see it.
Do not hold the baby upside down by the legs or shake them.
Do not give back blows to a baby who is coughing and crying well.
lessons.call: Call if the baby cannot breathe, cry or cough, or becomes unresponsive. A baby who needed back blows or chest thrusts should always be checked by a doctor.
special: Sit or kneel and rest your forearm on your thigh to support the baby securely.
Prevention: keep coins, button batteries, nuts, grapes and small toys out of reach.
A swallowed button battery or magnet is an emergency even if the baby seems fine: go to hospital now.
lessons.why: Babies have small airways that block easily. Holding the baby head down along your arm lets gravity help while back blows jolt the object loose. Chest thrusts squeeze the chest to force air out and push the object up. Abdominal thrusts are not used because a baby's liver and other organs are large and unprotected below the ribs and are easily injured. Supporting the jaw, not the soft throat, keeps the airway open. If the baby becomes unresponsive, CPR compressions also build pressure in the chest, help clear the airway and keep blood flowing. Even after success, a doctor should check for injury or small pieces left behind.

quiz.q: A 9-month-old is gagging on a piece of fruit and cannot cry or cough. What first?
options: 5 back blows, face down along your forearm, head low
quiz.why: Start with up to 5 back blows, with the baby head down along your arm and the jaw supported.

quiz.q: Back blows did not work. What comes next for a baby?
options: Chest thrusts on the lower breastbone
quiz.why: Babies get chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts. Then alternate back blows and chest thrusts.

quiz.q: The baby goes limp and stops responding. What now?
quiz.why: An unresponsive choking baby needs CPR. Look in the mouth before breaths and remove only what you can see.

sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025
AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Drowning
lessons.when: Someone is in trouble in water, or has been pulled out after struggling or going under.
recognize: Head low in the water, mouth at water level, tilted back
Upright with no kicking, arms pressing down, unable to wave or shout
Silent: drowning rarely looks like splashing and calling
After rescue: coughing, breathless, vomiting, confused or unresponsive
Not breathing or only gasping
steps: Shout for help and call emergency services (911 in the Philippines). Do not jump in unless trained.
Reach with a pole or towel, or throw something that floats. Keep low so you are not pulled in.
Once out, lay them on their back on firm ground. Check response and breathing.
Not breathing normally: open the airway and give 5 rescue breaths.
Then start CPR: 30 compressions, then 2 breaths. Keep going without long pauses.
If they vomit, roll them onto their side, clear the mouth, then roll back and continue.
Use an AED when it arrives: dry the chest first and follow its voice.
Breathing: use the recovery position, keep them warm, and keep checking breathing.
Everyone who needed rescue, breaths or CPR must go to hospital, even if they seem fine.
dont: Do not swim out to a panicking person unless trained; they can drag you under.
Do not try to drain water by pressing on the belly or holding them upside down.
Do not use hands-only CPR if you can give breaths; drowning victims need oxygen.
Do not let a rescued person go home without a medical check if they cough, feel breathless or drowsy.
lessons.call: Call for anyone struggling in water. Anyone who was unresponsive, needed breaths or CPR, or has a cough, breathlessness or confusion afterwards must go to hospital, as problems can develop hours later.
special: Alone with no phone: give about 1 minute of CPR before going for help (AHA advises about 2 minutes).
Children can drown silently in less than a minute in shallow water, buckets or baths: watch them constantly.
Diving or shallow-water injury: support the head and neck in line, but breathing and CPR come first.
lessons.why: Drowning stops breathing first, and the heart stops later because it runs out of oxygen. That is why breaths are vital and why European guidelines start with 5 rescue breaths before compressions. Pushing on the belly to remove water does not help: little water enters the lungs and it can cause vomiting and delay CPR. Vomiting is common, so turning the person to the side clears the mouth. Rescuers often drown trying to help, so reaching or throwing from land is far safer than swimming out. Water in the lungs can cause swelling and breathing trouble hours later, so anyone who needed rescue should be checked in hospital.

quiz.q: A teenager is pulled from a river, not breathing. What do you do first?
options: Press on his belly to get water out
Give 5 rescue breaths, then start CPR
Put him in the recovery position
quiz.why: Drowning causes a lack of oxygen. Give 5 rescue breaths, then 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

quiz.q: You see a child far out in a resort pool, head low and silent, not waving. You cannot swim well. What is best?
options: Jump in and swim to her
Shout for help, call, and reach or throw a floating object
Wait to see if she comes up
quiz.why: Reach or throw from the side so you do not become a victim too, and get trained help coming.

quiz.q: Your friend was rescued from the sea and coughed a lot, but now feels fine. What should he do?
options: Go to a doctor or hospital to be checked
quiz.why: Breathing problems can appear hours after a near drowning. He needs a medical check.

sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025

lessons.title: Severe bleeding
lessons.when: Blood is spurting, pouring or pooling, or soaking through clothing or dressings fast.
recognize: Blood spurting or flowing steadily from a wound
Blood pooling on the ground or soaking clothes quickly
Dressings soaking through within a minute or two
A limb partly or fully cut off
Pale, cold, sweaty skin, confusion or fainting (shock)
steps: Make sure the scene is safe, then put on gloves or use a plastic bag as a barrier if you can.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) or have someone call and bring a first aid kit.
Find the source of the bleeding; open or cut away clothing so you can see the wound.
Press hard directly on the wound with a clean cloth or dressing, using both hands and your body weight.
Keep pressing without lifting to check; if blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and press harder.
For an arm or leg that keeps bleeding, apply a tourniquet above the wound (see Tourniquet).
For a deep wound in the neck, armpit or groin, pack it tightly and press (see Wound packing).
Lay them down, keep them warm and stay with them until help takes over.
dont: Do not lift the dressing to look; each peek lets the bleeding restart.
Do not waste time raising the limb or pressing on pressure points; they do not reliably stop bleeding.
Do not remove soaked dressings; add more on top.
Do not give food or drink.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) at once for any bleeding you cannot quickly control, or any spurting blood.
special: Children have less blood to lose: treat bleeding that seems moderate in an adult as serious in a small child.
People on blood thinners (for example warfarin or newer anticoagulants) bleed longer; keep pressure on longer and get them checked.
lessons.why: A person can bleed to death within minutes, often before an ambulance arrives, so you are the real first responder. Firm, direct pressure squeezes the torn blood vessels shut and gives the body time to form a clot. Lifting the dressing tears that early clot away, which is why you keep pressing and add more layers instead. When pressure on an arm or leg is not enough, a tourniquet stops the flow upstream. Deep wounds where a limb joins the body cannot take a tourniquet, so you push gauze right onto the bleeding vessel and press. Raising the limb and pressure points are no longer taught because they do not work well and waste precious time.

quiz.q: A man has a deep cut on his forearm. Blood soaks through your first cloth within a minute. What do you do?
options: Add more cloth on top and press harder
Remove the soaked cloth and put on a clean one
Press on the inside of his upper arm instead
quiz.why: Removing the cloth disturbs the clot. Add layers and press harder; if it still bleeds, use a tourniquet.

quiz.q: You arrive at a motorbike crash and see blood pooling under a rider's thigh. What comes first after making sure traffic is controlled?
options: Look for a pulse in the foot
Call for help and press hard on the wound or apply a tourniquet
Move them to the side of the road before doing anything
quiz.why: Life-threatening bleeding kills in minutes. Get help coming and stop the bleeding right away.

quiz.q: How long should you keep pressing on a heavily bleeding wound?
options: Until the bleeding stops or professionals take over, without lifting to look
Only until the person stops complaining
quiz.why: Keep continuous firm pressure. Checking too early pulls off the forming clot.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons)

lessons.title: Tourniquet
lessons.when: Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that direct pressure is not controlling, or cannot be applied.
recognize: Spurting or steady heavy bleeding from an arm or leg
Bleeding continues despite firm direct pressure
A limb is cut off or badly crushed
You must leave to help others or cannot keep pressing
Several casualties and too few helpers
steps: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines), and get a commercial windlass tourniquet if one is available.
Place the band 5 to 7 cm above the wound, on the limb, never on a joint.
If the wound is at or just below a joint, place the tourniquet above that joint instead.
Pull the strap as tight as you can, then twist the windlass rod until the bleeding stops.
Lock the rod in its clip and secure the loose strap so nothing can unwind.
Write the time it was applied on the tourniquet or the person's forehead, and tell responders.
If bleeding continues, apply a second tourniquet just above the first and tighten it.
Never loosen or remove it yourself; leave it on and keep it visible, not covered by clothing.
dont: Do not use thin cord, wire, string or cable ties; they cut tissue and do not compress well.
Do not rely on a belt; it cannot be tightened enough without a windlass.
Do not loosen it to let blood flow back; the bleeding will restart.
Do not stop short because it hurts; a tight tourniquet is very painful and that is expected.
Do not place it over a knee or elbow.
lessons.call: Always call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) when you apply a tourniquet. The person needs a hospital urgently, and only the hospital team should remove it.
special: Commercial tourniquets work on children too; on a very small child's limb, firm direct pressure or packing may work better if the tourniquet cannot tighten enough.
Elderly people may have fragile skin; still apply it fully when bleeding is life-threatening.
lessons.why: A tourniquet squeezes the whole limb so hard that blood can no longer reach the wound. Too loose is dangerous: it blocks veins but not arteries, so the limb fills with blood and bleeds more. That is why you tighten until the bleeding stops, and the pain is a sign you did it right. A purpose-made windlass tourniquet is by far the most reliable. An improvised one can work if it is wide (a folded triangular bandage or cloth strip) and tightened with a strong stick twisted as a windlass, but many improvised tourniquets fail, and a belt alone rarely works. Limbs usually survive a few hours with a tourniquet, while a person can die from bleeding in minutes, so saving life comes first.

quiz.q: You have tightened a tourniquet on a thigh and the bleeding has slowed but not stopped. What next?
options: Loosen it slightly to reduce pain
Keep twisting until bleeding stops, then add a second tourniquet above if needed
Remove it and go back to pressure only
quiz.why: A tourniquet that only slows bleeding can make it worse. Tighten more and use a second one above if needed.

quiz.q: You have no tourniquet. Which improvised option is most likely to work?
options: A wide folded cloth tied around the limb and twisted tight with a strong stick
quiz.why: A wide band plus a windlass gives enough pressure. Narrow items cut in and belts rarely tighten enough. Keep pressing on the wound while you prepare it.

quiz.q: The wound is just below the knee. Where does the tourniquet go?
options: Just above the knee, on the thigh
quiz.why: Never put a tourniquet on a joint. Go above the joint, on the thigh.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons)

lessons.title: Wound packing
lessons.when: Heavy bleeding from a deep wound in the neck, armpit or groin, where a tourniquet cannot go.
recognize: Deep wound in the groin, armpit, neck or buttock
Steady or spurting bleeding that surface pressure does not stop
A wound large enough to push gauze or cloth into
Deep limb wound still bleeding after a tourniquet
steps: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) and put on gloves if you have them.
Use hemostatic gauze if you have it; otherwise plain gauze or a clean cloth.
Find where the blood comes from and push the gauze deep onto that spot with your fingers.
Keep feeding gauze in, packing it tightly until the whole wound is filled and gauze stands above the skin.
Press down hard on the packed wound with both hands and your body weight.
Hold firm pressure without lifting: at least 3 minutes for hemostatic gauze, about 10 minutes for plain gauze.
If blood still seeps, add more gauze on top and keep pressing; do not pull the packing out.
Once bleeding stops, bandage firmly over the packing and keep watching them for shock.
dont: Do not pack wounds of the chest or belly; just press on them and call.
Do not wrap a bandage tightly around the neck; it can choke them.
Do not remove packing to check; it pulls out the clot.
Do not only lay gauze on the surface; it must reach the bleeding point.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for every wound that needs packing. These are life-threatening injuries that need surgery.
special: In a child, use smaller amounts of gauze and the same firm pressure; small wounds can still hide large vessels.
For the neck, pack and press with your hand, keeping pressure off the windpipe.
lessons.why: Large blood vessels run close to the surface where the limbs and neck join the body. These junctional areas cannot take a tourniquet, and pressing on the skin alone often does not reach the vessel deep inside. Packing puts the gauze right against the bleeding point and fills the space so blood cannot collect. Your pressure on top then squeezes the vessel against the bone or firm tissue behind it. Hemostatic gauze contains a substance that speeds clotting, so it needs a shorter hold. Plain gauze or a clean cloth still works but needs longer pressure. Never pack the chest or belly because you could push gauze into body cavities.

timer.label: Hold pressure on the packed wound

quiz.q: A woman has a deep stab wound in her groin bleeding heavily. What is the best action?
options: Apply a tourniquet around her hip
Pack the wound tightly with gauze and press hard
Cover it loosely and keep her warm
quiz.why: Groin wounds are junctional: a tourniquet cannot go there. Pack deep and press firmly.

quiz.q: After packing with plain gauze, how long should you hold firm pressure?
options: No pressure is needed after packing
quiz.why: Plain gauze needs about 10 minutes of firm pressure. Hemostatic gauze needs at least 3.

quiz.q: Which wound should you NOT pack?
options: A deep wound in the armpit
A deep wound in the thigh
A deep wound in the groin
quiz.why: Do not pack chest or belly wounds. Press on them and call.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons)

lessons.title: Cuts and grazes
lessons.when: Small cuts, scrapes and grazes that stop bleeding with a few minutes of pressure.
recognize: Shallow cut or scrape that oozes rather than spurts
Bleeding stops after a few minutes of pressure
Dirt, sand or grit in a graze
Edges of the cut come together easily
steps: Wash your hands and wear gloves if you have them.
Press with a clean cloth for a few minutes to stop the bleeding.
Rinse the wound under clean running water, ideally drinkable tap water, until all dirt is gone.
Gently remove remaining grit with clean tweezers or by rinsing more; wash the skin around with soap.
Apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment or petroleum jelly if you have it.
Cover with a clean dressing or plaster and change it daily or when wet or dirty.
Check their tetanus vaccine: a booster is needed if it has been 10 years, or 5 for a dirty wound.
Watch it daily for signs of infection for the next few days.
dont: Do not pour alcohol or hydrogen peroxide into the wound; they damage healthy tissue.
Do not apply herbs, coffee grounds, toothpaste or other home remedies.
Do not leave sand or coral pieces in the wound.
Do not ignore increasing redness, swelling or pus.
lessons.call: See a doctor the same day for wounds that gape, are deep, will not stop bleeding after 10 minutes of pressure, are on the face, hands, genitals or joints, are very dirty, or come from bites, rusty or dirty objects, coral or floodwater. Get help urgently for spreading redness, red streaks, fever or feeling unwell.
special: Children: check that their routine vaccines, including tetanus, are up to date.
People with diabetes or poor circulation heal slowly and infect easily; have any foot wound checked.
Wading in floodwater with a wound risks leptospirosis; see a doctor, who may give preventive antibiotics.
lessons.why: Most small wounds heal well on their own if they are clean. Running water is the best cleaner because it flushes out dirt and germs, and plain drinkable tap water works as well as special solutions. Strong antiseptics like alcohol and hydrogen peroxide sting and harm the cells that repair the skin. A moist, covered wound heals faster and scars less than one left to dry. In hot, humid places such as Palawan, wounds get infected quickly, especially coral cuts, so daily checks matter. Signs of infection are increasing pain, redness, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaks spreading from the wound, or fever. Tetanus germs live in soil and can enter even small wounds, so keep the vaccine current.

quiz.q: Your friend scrapes their knee on coral while snorkelling. What is the best cleaning method?
options: Rinse with sea water and leave it open
Rinse well under clean running tap water, remove grit, cover it
quiz.why: Clean running water flushes out coral and germs. Coral cuts infect easily, so remove all pieces and cover the wound.

quiz.q: Two days after a cut, the area is hotter, more painful and a red line is spreading up the arm. What should you do?
options: Change the plaster and wait a week
quiz.why: Red streaks spreading from a wound suggest the infection is spreading. This needs prompt medical care.

quiz.q: A man steps on a rusty nail. His last tetanus shot was 7 years ago. What is right?
options: Tetanus only comes from rust, so clean the rust off
He should get a tetanus booster because the wound is dirty and it has been over 5 years
quiz.why: For dirty or puncture wounds, a booster is advised if more than 5 years have passed. Tetanus comes from soil germs, not rust itself.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Nosebleed
lessons.when: Bleeding from one or both nostrils, with or without a minor knock.
recognize: Blood dripping or running from the nose
Blood running down the back of the throat
Often starts after nose picking, blowing, dry air or a knock
May spit or cough up some blood that ran back
steps: Sit them down and have them lean forward, head tilted slightly down.
Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly, just below the bony bridge, closing both nostrils.
Hold the pinch continuously for 10 to 15 minutes; breathe through the mouth.
Have them spit out blood rather than swallow it.
If bleeding continues, pinch again for another 10 to 15 minutes.
Once stopped, avoid blowing the nose, bending over or heavy lifting for the rest of the day.
dont: Do not tilt the head back; blood runs into the throat and can cause vomiting or choking.
Do not lie them flat.
Do not keep letting go to check if it has stopped.
Do not pack the nose with tissue or cotton.
lessons.call: Get medical help if bleeding lasts more than 20 minutes despite good pressure, is very heavy, follows a hard blow to the head or face, or the person takes blood thinners. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if they feel faint, become pale and sweaty, or have trouble breathing.
special: Children get nosebleeds often and they are usually harmless; help them lean forward and pinch for them.
Older people and those on blood thinners or with high blood pressure may bleed longer and more often; seek care sooner.
lessons.why: Most nosebleeds come from small blood vessels at the front of the nose, just inside the soft part. Pinching that soft part squeezes those vessels shut. Pinching the bony bridge does nothing because it does not press on them. Clots take several minutes to form, so you need a long, steady pinch without peeking. Leaning forward lets blood drain out of the nose instead of down the throat, where swallowed blood can cause nausea and vomiting, which can restart the bleeding. A cold pack on the nose or neck is sometimes used, but evidence is weak; pressure is what works.

quiz.q: A child has a nosebleed. Which position is right?
options: Sitting with the head tilted back
quiz.why: Leaning forward keeps blood out of the throat and stomach.

quiz.q: Where should you pinch?
options: The hard bony bridge between the eyes
The soft fleshy part of the nose just below the bone
quiz.why: The bleeding vessels are in the soft front part of the nose, so that is where pressure works.

quiz.q: An elderly man on blood thinners has a nosebleed that has not stopped after 20 minutes of good pressure. What now?
options: Keep pinching for another hour at home
Have him blow his nose hard
quiz.why: A nosebleed lasting over 20 minutes, especially on blood thinners, needs medical care.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Impaled object
lessons.when: An object such as a knife, stick, metal rod, glass or fish spear is stuck in the body.
recognize: An object sticking out of a wound
Bleeding around the object
Pain and reluctance to move the area
Possible signs of shock: pale, sweaty, fast breathing
steps: Make sure the scene is safe and call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Leave the object where it is and keep the person still.
Press firmly around the object, on both sides, to control bleeding, never on the object itself.
Build up rolled cloths or bandages around the object so it cannot move.
Bandage over the padding to hold it in place, without pressing on the object.
If the object is very long, have it steadied; only trained rescuers should cut it shorter.
Help them into the most comfortable position, keep them warm and watch for shock.
Only remove it if it blocks their breathing or stops you from doing CPR.
dont: Do not pull the object out; it may be plugging a blood vessel.
Do not push on the object or let it move.
Do not give food or drink, in case surgery is needed.
Do not try to cut or break the object yourself.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for any object stuck in the body, except a small splinter or fish hook in the skin that is easily removed.
special: Keep a child calm and still; a parent holding them can help.
An object in the eye: do not press on it; cover both eyes loosely, with a cup over the object if possible, so the eyes do not move.
lessons.why: An object stuck in the body often presses on the blood vessels it has cut, acting like a plug. Pulling it out removes that plug and can cause sudden, heavy bleeding, and the edges may tear more tissue on the way out. Surgeons remove objects in hospital where they can control bleeding. Padding around the object stops it from rocking and doing more damage while you move or wait. Pressing on either side, not on the object, controls bleeding without driving it deeper. The only exception is when the object stops the person breathing or prevents CPR, because then breathing is the more immediate threat.

quiz.q: A fisherman has a large hook-tipped spear lodged in his thigh. What do you do?
options: Pull it out quickly to reduce pain
Leave it in, pad around it, press around it and call
Push it through the other side
Cut it flush with the skin
quiz.why: Leave it in place and stabilise it. Removing it can cause major bleeding.

quiz.q: Where should you press to control bleeding?
options: Around the object, on either side
quiz.why: Press beside the object so you control bleeding without driving it deeper.

quiz.q: When may a layperson remove an impaled object?
options: When it blocks breathing or prevents CPR
quiz.why: Breathing and CPR come first. Otherwise leave it for the hospital.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Amputation
lessons.when: A finger, toe, hand, foot or limb has been fully or partly cut or torn off.
recognize: Part of the body cut or torn off
Part hanging by skin or tissue
Heavy bleeding, or sometimes surprisingly little
Severe pain, or numbness
Signs of shock: pale, cold, sweaty, confused
steps: Make sure the scene is safe, switch off machinery, and call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Stop the bleeding first: firm pressure, and a tourniquet above the wound if a limb bleeds heavily.
Cover the stump with a clean, damp dressing and bandage it firmly.
For a partial amputation, keep the part in line with the limb, support it and dress it as one.
Find the severed part; rinse off dirt gently with clean water, but do not scrub it.
Wrap the part in damp clean gauze or cloth and seal it in a plastic bag.
Place the bag in a second bag or container with ice and water, so the part does not touch ice.
Label it with the person's name and time of injury, and send it with them to hospital.
Keep the person lying down and warm, and watch for shock.
dont: Do not put the part directly on ice or in ice water; freezing destroys it.
Do not soak the part in water or put it in alcohol or any chemical.
Do not delay bleeding control to search for the part.
Do not try to reattach or cut off a partly attached part.
lessons.call: Always call emergency services (911 in the Philippines). Reattachment is time-sensitive, so tell them about the amputation; they may route you to a hospital with a surgical team.
special: Children's fingertips often heal well; always bring the tip to hospital even if small.
Clean cuts reattach better than crush or tear injuries, but always bring the part: the surgeon decides.
lessons.why: Life comes before limb, so the bleeding is always the first priority. Torn arteries may spasm and bleed little at first, then suddenly bleed heavily, so watch closely. A severed part can sometimes be reattached, but only if its tissue stays alive. Keeping it cool slows the damage, like keeping food fresh. Direct contact with ice freezes and destroys the cells, while soaking it in water makes the tissue swell and become harder to repair. A sealed bag in a cool bath of ice and water is the safe middle path. Labelling it with the time helps surgeons decide whether reattachment is possible.

quiz.q: A worker's finger is cut off by a machine. How should you transport the finger?
options: Directly on a block of ice
Wrapped in damp gauze, in a sealed bag, placed in ice and water
In alcohol to keep it clean
quiz.why: Keep the part cool but never in direct contact with ice or soaking in fluid.

quiz.q: A leg is severed and bleeding heavily. What is your first priority?
options: Stop the bleeding with a tourniquet and pressure
quiz.why: Life before limb. Control bleeding first.

quiz.q: A finger is hanging by a strip of skin. What should you do?
options: Cut the strip so it can be bagged
Keep it in place, support it in its normal position and dress it
quiz.why: That strip may carry blood vessels. Keep everything in place for the surgeon.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Open chest wound
lessons.when: A stab, gunshot or puncture wound to the chest or upper back.
recognize: Wound in the chest, upper back or under the armpit
Sucking or hissing sound as they breathe
Bubbling or frothy blood at the wound
Increasing shortness of breath or chest pain
Coughing up blood, pale or bluish skin
steps: Make sure the scene is safe and call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Leave the wound open to the air; do not seal it with plastic or tape.
If it bleeds, press on it with your gloved hand or a clean non-airtight dressing such as gauze.
Leave any object in the wound in place and pad around it.
If they are awake, help them sit up or find the position that makes breathing easiest.
If they become unresponsive but breathe normally, place them in the recovery position, injured side down.
Watch their breathing closely; if a dressing is on and breathing worsens, remove or loosen the dressing.
If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.
dont: Do not tape plastic or other airtight material over the wound.
Do not pack a chest wound.
Do not give food or drink.
Do not remove an object stuck in the chest.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) at once for any wound to the chest or upper back, even if it looks small.
special: Children may hide how hard they are breathing; watch for fast breathing, flaring nostrils and drowsiness.
In pregnancy, a wound to the lower chest may also involve the belly; call and keep her on her left side if lying down.
lessons.why: A wound in the chest can let air into the space around the lung, so the lung collapses. Older courses taught laypeople to seal the wound with plastic taped on three sides. Current guidelines (AHA, Red Cross, ERC) advise laypeople not to do this, because an airtight cover can trap air inside the chest. That trapped air builds pressure, squashes the lung and heart, and can kill quickly (tension pneumothorax). An open wound lets that air escape. So leave it open, or use a plain dressing that air can pass through, and press only to stop bleeding. If breathing gets worse, take the dressing off. Trained professionals may use special vented chest seals, but that is their job.

quiz.q: A man has a small stab wound to his chest that makes a sucking sound. What is current advice for laypeople?
options: Tape plastic tightly over it on all sides
Have him lie flat on his back and walk later
Leave it open or cover it with a non-airtight dressing, and call
quiz.why: Airtight seals can trap air and cause a deadly pressure build-up. Leave it open or use a breathable dressing.

quiz.q: You put gauze on a chest wound and the person's breathing is getting worse. What should you do?
options: Add more layers and press harder
quiz.why: Worsening breathing can mean trapped air. Removing the dressing lets it escape.

quiz.q: A conscious person has a chest wound and is struggling to breathe. Which position?
options: Sitting up or in whatever position eases breathing
quiz.why: Sitting up usually makes breathing easier; let them choose what is most comfortable.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Shock and internal bleeding
lessons.when: Someone is pale, cold, sweaty and weak after bleeding, injury, burns, severe illness or a severe allergy.
recognize: Pale or grey, cold, clammy skin
Fast, weak pulse and fast, shallow breathing
Anxiety, confusion, drowsiness or restlessness
Thirst, nausea, dizziness or fainting
Internal bleeding: swollen, hard or tender belly, or large bruises after injury
Vomiting or coughing blood, black tarry stools, or blood in urine
steps: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) right away.
Treat the cause you can: stop external bleeding, or give an adrenaline auto-injector for anaphylaxis.
Lay them flat on their back on a blanket or mat.
If uninjured legs and no pain, you may raise the legs a little; stop if it causes discomfort.
Loosen tight clothing and keep them warm with a blanket over and under them.
Give nothing to eat or drink; you may moisten their lips if they are thirsty.
Reassure them, stay with them, and check their breathing and alertness every few minutes.
If they become unresponsive but breathe normally, use the recovery position; if not breathing normally, start CPR.
dont: Do not let them sit up, stand or walk around.
Do not give food, water or alcohol.
Do not raise the legs if you suspect leg, hip, spine or head injury.
Do not overheat them with hot water bottles or heaters.
Do not leave them alone.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) at once for any signs of shock, or any suspected internal bleeding after a fall, crash, blow to the belly or chest, or in pregnancy.
special: Children can look fine and then collapse suddenly; a fast heartbeat, pale skin and drowsiness are early warnings.
Dengue is common in South-East Asia: belly pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, or drowsiness as fever settles mean shock may come; go to hospital now.
Pregnancy: lay her tilted on her left side; in early pregnancy, belly pain with fainting can mean internal bleeding (ectopic pregnancy).
lessons.why: Shock means the body's organs are not getting enough blood and oxygen. The most common cause after injury is blood loss, either outside or hidden inside the belly, chest or thigh. The body first copes by speeding up the heart and pulling blood away from the skin, which is why the skin turns pale, cold and sweaty. Later the brain suffers, causing confusion and drowsiness. Lying flat helps blood reach the brain and heart. Raising uninjured legs can give a short boost, but guidelines say it is only a temporary measure and not proven to help outcomes. Keeping warm matters because cold makes bleeding worse. Food and drink are avoided because they may need surgery. Only hospital care can fix shock.

quiz.q: After a motorbike crash, a rider has no visible bleeding but is pale, sweaty, confused and has a tender, swollen belly. What is likely happening?
options: Internal bleeding causing shock: call emergency services now
quiz.why: Signs of shock with a tender belly after a crash suggest internal bleeding, which needs surgery fast.

quiz.q: A person in shock asks for water. What do you do?
options: Give nothing to drink, but you may moisten their lips
Give coffee to raise blood pressure
quiz.why: They may need surgery and can vomit. Moisten the lips only.

quiz.q: Which is the best position for someone in shock with no spine, leg or head injury?
options: Lying flat, legs raised a little if comfortable
quiz.why: Lying flat supports blood flow to the brain. Raising uninjured legs briefly is optional.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Heart attack
lessons.when: Chest pain, pressure or discomfort that could be the heart, especially lasting more than a few minutes.
recognize: Pressure, squeezing, tightness or pain in the centre of the chest, lasting minutes or coming back
Pain spreading to an arm, the neck, jaw, back or upper belly
Shortness of breath, with or without chest pain
Cold sweat, nausea or vomiting, light-headedness
Pale or grey skin, anxiety, a feeling that something is very wrong
Women, older people and diabetics may have only breathlessness, tiredness, nausea or vague discomfort
steps: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) now. Do not wait to see if it passes.
Help them sit or rest in the position they find most comfortable, often half sitting with knees bent.
Loosen tight clothing and keep them calm. Do not let them walk around or drive themselves.
If they are an adult, not allergic and not told to avoid it, give one aspirin (often 300 mg) to chew.
If they have their own prescribed nitroglycerin (GTN) spray or tablet, help them take it as directed.
Ask someone to find an AED (defibrillator) and bring it, just in case.
Stay with them, keep checking their breathing and note when the pain started.
If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, start CPR and use the AED as soon as it arrives.
dont: Do not let them brush it off as indigestion or wait for it to pass.
Do not give aspirin to a child, to someone allergic to it, with a bleeding problem, or who may be having a stroke.
Do not give them someone else's heart medicine.
Do not let them drive themselves to hospital.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) at once for any chest pain or pressure that could be the heart. If no ambulance can come quickly, get them to the nearest hospital with an emergency department by car, driven by someone else.
special: Women, older people and people with diabetes often have no classic chest pain: take breathlessness, nausea, sweating or unusual tiredness seriously.
Aspirin dose varies by country: often 300 mg in Europe and Asia, 162 to 325 mg in the US. Chewing makes it work faster.
lessons.why: A heart attack usually happens when a blood clot blocks an artery feeding the heart muscle. Every minute without blood flow, more muscle dies, so calling early matters most: hospitals can open the artery, but only if they get the person in time. Resting lowers the heart's work and oxygen need. Chewed aspirin thins the blood and helps stop the clot from growing; chewing gets it into the blood faster than swallowing it whole. A heart attack can trigger cardiac arrest, where the heart stops pumping. That is why you keep an AED nearby and watch their breathing: CPR and an early shock are what keep someone alive until help arrives.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old man has had heavy chest pressure for 10 minutes and is sweating. He says it is probably indigestion. What do you do first?
options: Give him an antacid and wait 30 minutes
quiz.why: Chest pressure with sweating is a heart attack until proven otherwise. Calling early gets treatment to the heart muscle fastest.

quiz.q: She is an adult with suspected heart attack, not allergic to aspirin and has no bleeding problems. How should she take aspirin?
options: Swallow it whole with lots of water
Take it only after the ambulance arrives
Dissolve it under the tongue for an hour
quiz.why: Chewing gets aspirin into the blood faster, helping to limit the clot.

quiz.q: While you wait, the man collapses, does not respond and is only gasping. What now?
options: Put him in the recovery position
Start CPR and use an AED as soon as it arrives
quiz.why: Gasping is not normal breathing. This is cardiac arrest: CPR and an early shock save lives.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025

lessons.title: Stroke
lessons.when: Sudden weakness, numbness, confusion, loss of balance or vision, or trouble speaking.
recognize: Balance: sudden dizziness, loss of balance or coordination
Eyes: sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes, or double vision
Face: one side of the face droops, uneven smile
Arms: one arm or leg is weak or numb, drifts down when both are raised
Speech: slurred, strange or confused speech, or cannot understand you
Sudden severe headache unlike any before
steps: Check BE FAST: ask them to smile, raise both arms and repeat a simple sentence.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) at once, even if the signs seem to fade.
Note the time they were last seen well. Tell the paramedics or hospital.
Keep them still and comfortable, sitting or lying with head and shoulders slightly raised.
Give nothing to eat or drink, not even water or medicine. Swallowing may be affected.
If they become unresponsive but breathe normally, put them in the recovery position, weak side down if you can.
Stay with them, reassure them and keep checking their breathing.
If they stop breathing normally, start CPR and get an AED.
dont: Do not wait to see if the signs go away.
Do not give aspirin: some strokes are caused by bleeding, which aspirin makes worse.
Do not give food, drink or tablets by mouth.
Do not let them drive or go to sleep it off.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) immediately for any BE FAST sign, even if it lasts only minutes. Ask to go to a hospital that can treat stroke.
special: Signs that come and go (a mini stroke, or TIA) still need emergency care the same day: a major stroke may follow.
Low blood sugar can look like a stroke. In a known diabetic who can swallow safely, sugar may help, but still call.
lessons.why: A stroke is a brain attack: a blood vessel in the brain is blocked by a clot or bursts and bleeds. Brain cells start dying within minutes, and some powerful hospital treatments only work within the first few hours. The time last seen well decides which treatments are safe, which is why you write it down. BE FAST helps you spot it quickly. Nothing by mouth matters because a stroke can weaken the swallowing muscles, so food or water may go into the lungs. Aspirin is left out because, until a scan is done, nobody knows whether the stroke is a clot or a bleed.

quiz.q: Your aunt suddenly cannot lift her right arm and her words are slurred. After 5 minutes she seems a bit better. What do you do?
options: Let her rest and see how she is tomorrow
Call emergency services now and note when the signs began
quiz.why: Signs that improve still need emergency care. The time of onset guides treatment.

quiz.q: A man with stroke signs asks for a glass of water. What do you do?
options: Give him water through a straw
Give him his usual tablets with water
quiz.why: Swallowing may be weakened, so drinks can enter the lungs.

quiz.q: What does the T in BE FAST stand for?
options: Time: call now and note when it started
quiz.why: Time is brain. Call at once and record when they were last seen well.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Anaphylaxis
lessons.when: A severe allergic reaction affecting breathing, the throat or circulation, often minutes after a food, sting or medicine.
recognize: Swelling of the tongue, lips or throat, hoarse voice, trouble swallowing
Wheezing, noisy breathing, persistent cough, shortness of breath
Pale, floppy, dizzy, faint or collapsing (low blood pressure)
Often with hives, itchy rash or flushing, but skin signs can be absent
Vomiting or stomach cramps after an insect sting or known allergen
Sudden onset, usually minutes to an hour after contact with the trigger
steps: Give their adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector into the outer thigh at once, through clothing if needed.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) and say anaphylaxis.
Lay them flat with legs raised. If breathing is hard, let them sit up instead.
Never let them stand up or walk, even if they feel better.
Remove the trigger if you can, such as scraping out a bee sting.
If there is no improvement after 5 minutes, give a second auto-injector if available.
If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, start CPR.
Even if they recover, they must go to hospital: symptoms can come back hours later.
dont: Do not delay adrenaline to give an antihistamine or inhaler first.
Do not let them stand, walk or sit up suddenly: this can cause collapse.
Do not worry about giving adrenaline when unsure: it is safer to give it than to wait.
Do not leave them alone.
lessons.call: Always call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for anaphylaxis, even if the adrenaline works. They need hospital observation.
special: Children have smaller junior auto-injectors; use theirs, or an adult one if it is all you have and it is life-threatening.
Pregnancy: lay them on their left side rather than flat on the back.
People with asthma and food allergies are at higher risk of severe reactions.
lessons.why: In anaphylaxis, the immune system overreacts across the whole body. Blood vessels widen and leak, so blood pressure falls, and airways swell and tighten. Adrenaline reverses all of this within minutes: it squeezes blood vessels, opens the airways and reduces swelling. That is why it comes first and fast; antihistamines are too slow and only help itching. Lying flat with legs raised helps blood reach the heart and brain. Standing up suddenly can make blood pool in the legs and the heart can empty and stop. Adrenaline wears off, and some reactions return, so a second dose and hospital care may be needed.

quiz.q: After eating peanuts, a friend's lips swell and she starts wheezing. She has an auto-injector. What first?
options: Use the auto-injector in her outer thigh now
quiz.why: Breathing problems after an allergen mean anaphylaxis. Adrenaline comes first.

quiz.q: Five minutes after adrenaline she is no better. You have a second auto-injector. What do you do?
options: Only give it if she collapses
Give it into the arm instead
quiz.why: A second dose is advised if there is no improvement after 5 to 15 minutes.

quiz.q: She feels better and wants to stand and go home. What do you advise?
options: Stay lying or sitting and go to hospital
Walk around to clear her head
Take a shower to cool down
quiz.why: Standing can cause sudden collapse, and symptoms can come back. Hospital observation is needed.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Allergic reaction
lessons.when: Itchy rash, hives, mild swelling or sneezing after a food, sting, plant or medicine, with normal breathing.
recognize: Itchy raised rash (hives) or red, blotchy skin
Mild swelling of the eyes, lips or face
Sneezing, runny nose, itchy or watery eyes
Tingling or itching in the mouth
Mild stomach upset
Breathing, voice and alertness all normal
steps: Stop contact with the trigger: stop eating, remove stingers, wash plant sap off the skin.
Check for danger signs: breathing trouble, throat or tongue swelling, hoarse voice, dizziness or fainting.
If any danger sign appears, treat as anaphylaxis: adrenaline auto-injector if they have one and call emergency services.
For mild symptoms, an antihistamine tablet or syrup can help itching. Follow the pack dose.
A cool compress can ease itchy, swollen skin.
Stay with them and watch closely for the next few hours.
Advise them to see a doctor to find the cause and ask about carrying an auto-injector.
dont: Do not rely on antihistamines if breathing, throat or circulation are affected.
Do not leave them alone right after the reaction starts.
Do not give them more of the suspected trigger to test it.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if any breathing difficulty, throat or tongue swelling, hoarse voice, collapse or severe dizziness appears. See a doctor the same day for facial swelling or a first-time reaction.
special: Children may not describe symptoms well: watch for a change in voice, drooling, floppiness or distress.
A mild reaction does not mean the next one will be mild. Someone with a past severe reaction needs close watching.
lessons.why: A mild allergic reaction stays in one area, mostly the skin, nose and eyes. Antihistamines block histamine, one of the chemicals that causes itching and hives, so they help these mild symptoms. But mild reactions can turn into anaphylaxis, sometimes quickly, when the reaction spreads to the airway or blood pressure. Antihistamines are too slow to stop that, which is why you keep checking for breathing, voice and dizziness, and switch to adrenaline and an emergency call the moment any danger sign appears. Removing the trigger quickly reduces how much allergen gets into the body.

quiz.q: A boy gets hives after a bee sting but breathes normally and is chatting. What do you do?
options: Remove the sting, consider an antihistamine and watch him closely
quiz.why: Hives alone with normal breathing is a mild reaction. Watch for danger signs.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes later his voice becomes hoarse and he feels dizzy. What now?
options: Treat as anaphylaxis: adrenaline if available and call emergency services
Let him lie down and sleep
quiz.why: A hoarse voice and dizziness mean the airway and circulation are involved: this is anaphylaxis.

quiz.q: Why is an antihistamine not enough for anaphylaxis?
options: It is too slow and does not open airways or raise blood pressure
quiz.why: Only adrenaline quickly reverses airway swelling and low blood pressure.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Asthma attack
lessons.when: Someone with asthma, or likely asthma, is wheezing, coughing or struggling to breathe.
recognize: Wheezing, coughing, chest tightness
Short of breath, breathing fast
Difficulty speaking in full sentences
Using shoulder and neck muscles to breathe, sucking in between the ribs
Anxiety, sweating; in severe cases blue lips, exhaustion or confusion
steps: Help them sit upright, leaning slightly forward. Stay calm and loosen tight clothing.
Help them use their reliever inhaler (usually blue, salbutamol), with a spacer if available.
Give 1 puff every 30 to 60 seconds, up to 10 puffs, shaking the inhaler before each puff.
If they are not better after 10 puffs, or worse at any time, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
If help has not arrived after about 10 minutes, repeat up to 10 puffs.
If they also have allergy signs and an adrenaline auto-injector, use it first.
If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, start CPR.
dont: Do not lay them flat: sitting up makes breathing easier.
Do not use a preventer (brown, orange or purple) inhaler for an attack; use the reliever.
Do not leave them alone or let them walk to get help.
Do not assume they are fine because wheezing stops: a silent chest can mean very little air is moving.
