lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if there is no improvement after 10 puffs, if it is getting worse, if they cannot speak, have blue lips, are exhausted or drowsy, or have no inhaler.
special: Children: use a spacer, with a face mask for young children. Follow the child's written asthma plan if they have one.
Plans differ by country, such as 4 puffs every 4 minutes in Australia. Follow the person's own written plan if they have one.
Pregnancy: asthma treatment is safe and important; treat the attack the same way.
lessons.why: In an asthma attack, the small airways tighten, swell and fill with mucus, so air struggles to get out. The reliever medicine relaxes the muscles around the airways within minutes. A spacer holds the medicine so it is breathed deep into the lungs instead of hitting the back of the throat, which makes each puff work much better. Giving puffs one at a time, spaced out, lets each one reach the airways. Sitting upright and leaning forward lets the breathing muscles work best. A quiet chest in someone struggling is a danger sign, not a good one: it can mean very little air is moving.

quiz.q: A woman with asthma is wheezing and struggling to speak. She has her blue inhaler and a spacer. How do you help?
options: Lay her flat and give 2 puffs
Sit her up and give 1 puff every 30 to 60 seconds, up to 10
quiz.why: Upright position and spaced puffs through a spacer let the medicine reach the airways.

quiz.q: After 10 puffs she is no better. What now?
options: Call emergency services and keep following the plan
Give her the brown preventer inhaler
Take her for a walk outside
quiz.why: No improvement after 10 puffs is an emergency. Repeat the puffs if help takes about 10 minutes.

quiz.q: Her wheezing goes quiet, but she looks exhausted and her lips are bluish. What does this mean?
options: This is very serious: very little air may be moving
quiz.why: A silent chest with blue lips means a life-threatening attack. Make sure help is coming and be ready for CPR.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Seizure
lessons.when: Someone is jerking, stiff, or suddenly unaware and unresponsive in a way that looks like a fit.
recognize: Sudden collapse, stiffening, then jerking of arms and legs
Not responding, eyes may roll or stare
Noisy breathing, drooling, biting the tongue, loss of bladder control
Some seizures are just staring, lip smacking or confused wandering
Afterwards: drowsy, confused, headache, may sleep
steps: Start timing the seizure now.
Move hard or sharp objects away. Cushion their head with something soft, like a folded jacket.
Loosen tight clothing around the neck and remove glasses.
Let the jerking happen. Do not hold them down or put anything in their mouth.
When the jerking stops, check breathing and put them in the recovery position.
Stay with them, talk calmly and let them rest until fully awake.
If they have an emergency medicine plan, such as buccal midazolam, follow it if you are trained.
If they are not breathing normally after the seizure ends, start CPR.
dont: Do not put anything in their mouth: they cannot swallow their tongue.
Do not restrain them or try to stop the movements.
Do not give food, drink or tablets until they are fully alert.
Do not move them unless they are in danger, such as near water, traffic or fire.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, another starts, they are injured, it happened in water, they are pregnant or diabetic, it is their first seizure, or they do not wake up.
special: Young children with a high fever may have a febrile seizure. Do not put them in a cold bath. Seek medical advice.
Pregnancy: a seizure in pregnancy is always an emergency, especially late in pregnancy or after birth.
In water: support their head above the water, get them out once the jerking stops and always call.
lessons.why: A seizure is a burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Most stop on their own within a few minutes, and your job is to stop injury while it runs its course. Holding someone down can cause bruises or broken bones, and putting things in the mouth can break teeth or block the airway; people cannot swallow their tongue. Timing matters because a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is less likely to stop on its own and needs medicine. The recovery position afterwards keeps the airway open and lets saliva or vomit drain out while they are drowsy.

quiz.q: A man collapses and starts jerking on a concrete floor. Someone wants to put a spoon in his mouth. What do you do?
options: Put the spoon in to protect his tongue
Stop them, cushion his head, clear the area and time the seizure
quiz.why: Nothing goes in the mouth. Protect from injury and time it.

quiz.q: The jerking has gone on for 6 minutes. What do you do?
options: Try to wake him with cold water
quiz.why: A seizure over 5 minutes needs emergency treatment.

quiz.q: The seizure stops. He is breathing but very drowsy. What next?
options: Sit him up and give coffee
Put him in the recovery position and stay with him
quiz.why: The recovery position keeps the airway clear while he recovers.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Low blood sugar
lessons.when: A person with diabetes, or who has not eaten, becomes shaky, sweaty, confused or acts strangely.
recognize: Shaking, sweating, pale skin, fast heartbeat
Hunger, headache, dizziness
Confusion, odd behaviour, irritability, seeming drunk
Slurred speech, poor coordination
Drowsiness, seizure or unresponsiveness in severe cases
Known diabetic on insulin or tablets, after missing a meal or exercising
steps: If they are alert and can swallow safely, give 15 to 20 g of fast sugar now.
Examples: glucose tablets (check the pack), about 150 to 200 mL of regular juice or soft drink, or sweets.
Let them sit down and rest. Stay with them.
Recheck after 15 minutes. If they are not better, give another 15 to 20 g of sugar.
Once better, give a snack or meal with longer-lasting carbohydrate, such as bread, crackers or rice.
If they cannot swallow safely or are drowsy, give nothing by mouth and call emergency services.
If unresponsive but breathing, put them in the recovery position. If trained, give their glucagon.
If they are not breathing normally, start CPR.
dont: Do not give food or drink to someone who is drowsy, unresponsive or cannot swallow.
Do not use diet or sugar-free drinks: they contain no sugar.
Do not give extra insulin.
Do not leave them alone until they are fully recovered and have eaten.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if they cannot swallow, become drowsy or unresponsive, have a seizure, or are not improving after two doses of sugar.
special: Children: smaller amounts of sugar are enough. Follow their diabetes care plan if they have one.
If unsure whether blood sugar is high or low, giving sugar to someone alert is safe and may help.
Older people and people with long-term diabetes may have few warning signs.
lessons.why: The brain runs almost entirely on sugar from the blood. When blood sugar falls too low, often after too much insulin, a missed meal or exercise, the brain starts to fail, causing confusion and eventually unconsciousness or seizures. Fast sugar is absorbed quickly and usually helps within 10 to 15 minutes, which is why you recheck at 15 minutes. A longer-lasting snack afterwards stops the sugar from dropping again. Someone who is drowsy cannot protect their airway, so food or drink may go into their lungs: they need emergency care and, if available, a glucagon injection or spray.

quiz.q: A diabetic colleague is sweaty, shaky and confused but can talk and swallow. What do you give?
options: 15 to 20 g of fast sugar, such as glucose tablets or regular juice
Nothing until a doctor sees her
quiz.why: Fast sugar quickly corrects low blood sugar in someone who can swallow safely.

quiz.q: Fifteen minutes later she is still confused. What now?
options: Give another 15 to 20 g of sugar and consider calling
Give her a large meal immediately
quiz.why: Repeat the sugar if not improving. Call if she gets worse or does not improve.

quiz.q: A diabetic man is drowsy and cannot swallow properly. What do you do?
options: Give nothing by mouth, recovery position and call emergency services
Give him a sweet to suck
Sit him up and give water
quiz.why: Anything by mouth could enter the lungs. He needs emergency treatment.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Fainting
lessons.when: Someone feels faint or briefly collapses and wakes up within a minute or so.
recognize: Feeling light-headed, dizzy, weak or about to faint
Pale, sweaty, nauseous, blurred or tunnel vision
Brief collapse, then waking up quickly once lying down
Often after standing a long time, heat, pain, fear, the sight of blood, or getting up quickly
steps: If they feel faint, help them lie down or sit, ideally lying with legs raised.
If they cannot lie down, crossing the legs and tensing leg, belly and buttock muscles can help.
If they have collapsed, check that they respond and are breathing normally.
If unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) and start CPR.
If breathing but not waking within a minute or so, put them in the recovery position and call.
Once awake, keep them lying down for a while, then sit up slowly before standing.
Check for injuries from the fall, especially to the head.
Move to a cool place and give sips of water once fully alert.
dont: Do not sit them up or stand them up quickly.
Do not splash water or slap them to wake them.
Do not give food or drink until fully alert.
Do not assume every faint is harmless, especially without warning signs.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if they do not wake quickly, faint during exercise or with no warning, have chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness, are injured, pregnant or older, or faint again.
special: Pregnancy: lie them on their left side rather than flat on the back, and get medical advice.
Older people: fainting may be from heart problems or medicines and should be checked by a doctor.
In tropical heat, fainting may be heat exhaustion: move to shade, cool them and give fluids.
lessons.why: A simple faint happens when the heart rate and blood pressure drop for a moment, so too little blood reaches the brain. Lying down with the legs raised brings blood back to the brain, and most people wake within seconds. Tensing the muscles of the legs and belly squeezes blood back towards the heart and can stop a faint before it happens. Getting up too fast can cause another faint. Some collapses are not simple faints: during exercise, with chest pain or with no warning, the cause may be the heart. That is why you check breathing first and call if anything seems unusual.

quiz.q: A teenager in a hot church says she feels dizzy and her vision is going grey. What do you do?
options: Tell her to stand still and breathe
Help her lie down with legs raised
Give her a cup of coffee
quiz.why: Lying down with legs raised restores blood flow to the brain and prevents a fall.

quiz.q: A man collapses while jogging and wakes after a few seconds. He says he feels fine. What do you advise?
options: Call emergency services: fainting during exercise can be a heart problem
quiz.why: Fainting during exercise is a red flag for a heart cause.

quiz.q: Someone collapses and is not responding and only gasping. What do you do?
options: Call emergency services and start CPR
Put them in the recovery position
quiz.why: Gasping is not normal breathing: this is cardiac arrest, not a simple faint.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Poisoning
lessons.when: Someone has swallowed, breathed in or touched a medicine, chemical, plant or other harmful substance.
recognize: Open containers, spilled pills or chemicals nearby
Burns or stains around the mouth, unusual breath smell
Vomiting, stomach pain, drooling
Drowsiness, confusion, seizures or unresponsiveness
Breathing problems, sweating, small pupils (some pesticides)
May look completely well at first, for example after a paracetamol overdose
steps: Make sure the area is safe. For fumes, get fresh air in and do not enter if you may be overcome.
If they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR, using a barrier if available.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) or a poison centre, and follow their advice.
Find out what, how much and when. Keep the container, label or plant to show the medics.
If a chemical is in the mouth, have them rinse and spit. Give nothing to drink unless advised.
On skin or in eyes, remove contaminated clothing with gloves and flush with plenty of running water.
If they vomit or become drowsy, put them in the recovery position and keep checking breathing.
Stay with them until help arrives, even if they seem well.
dont: Do not make them vomit: it can burn the throat again or send poison into the lungs.
Do not give salt water, milk, oil or home remedies.
Do not give activated charcoal unless a poison centre or doctor tells you to.
Do not touch pesticides, chemicals or vomit with bare hands.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for any poisoning with symptoms or drowsiness. If they seem well, still call a poison centre, such as the National Poison Management and Control Center at UP-PGH in Manila, or go to hospital.
special: Children: even one or two adult tablets, or a sip of kerosene, bleach or a button battery, can be dangerous. Go to hospital.
Kerosene, petrol and lamp oil can enter the lungs if vomited: never induce vomiting.
Farm pesticide poisoning is common in South-East Asia: protect yourself, wash their skin and get to hospital fast.
lessons.why: Poisons harm the body in different ways, so the safest first aid is to stop more exposure, protect the airway and get expert advice fast. Poison centres and emergency services know the treatment for specific substances, which is why the container and the time matter. Making someone vomit is no longer advised: it rarely removes much poison, can burn the throat a second time with corrosives, and can push poison into the lungs. Rinsing the mouth or skin removes what has not yet been absorbed. Some poisons, such as paracetamol, cause no signs for many hours while damage builds silently, so people who seem fine still need care.

quiz.q: A toddler has drunk some liquid drain cleaner. What should you do?
options: Rinse his mouth, keep the bottle, call emergency services or a poison centre
Wait to see if symptoms develop
quiz.why: Do not induce vomiting. Rinse, keep the label and get expert help fast.

quiz.q: A farmer is confused and sweating after spraying pesticide. His clothes are soaked. What first?
options: Hug him to calm him down
With gloves, remove contaminated clothing, wash his skin and call emergency services
Let him rest in the field
quiz.why: Protect yourself and stop further absorption through the skin.

quiz.q: A woman took a handful of paracetamol an hour ago but feels fine. What do you advise?
options: Go to hospital now: damage can build without early signs
Give her charcoal from the fire
quiz.why: Paracetamol overdose can damage the liver before any symptoms appear. Early treatment works best.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
WHO guidance on poisoning prevention and management

lessons.title: Overdose
lessons.when: Someone may have taken too much opioid, drugs or alcohol and is very drowsy, unresponsive or breathing poorly.
recognize: Cannot be woken, or very drowsy and confused
Slow, shallow, noisy or no breathing; snoring or gurgling sounds
Blue or grey lips and fingertips, cold clammy skin
Opioids: very small (pinpoint) pupils
Alcohol: vomiting while barely awake, seizures, very low body temperature
Pills, needles, bottles or drug packets nearby
steps: Shout and firmly rub their breastbone to try to wake them. Check breathing.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines). Say they are not breathing properly or cannot be woken.
If opioids are possible and you have naloxone, give it: one nasal spray into one nostril.
If not breathing normally, give CPR. Rescue breaths are especially important for opioid overdose.
If no response in 2 to 3 minutes, give another naloxone dose, in the other nostril.
If breathing normally, put them in the recovery position and keep checking breathing.
Stay with them until help arrives: naloxone can wear off before the drug does.
For alcohol, keep them warm and on their side. Never leave them to sleep it off.
dont: Do not leave them alone to sleep it off.
Do not give coffee, cold showers or make them vomit.
Do not give more alcohol or drugs to calm them.
Do not delay calling for fear of trouble: say what was taken so medics can treat it.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for anyone who cannot be woken, is breathing slowly or noisily, has blue lips, a seizure, or has taken an unknown amount. Go to hospital for vision problems after drinking spirits.
special: Naloxone is safe and will not harm someone who has not taken opioids. It may be hard to get in the Philippines without a prescription.
Bootleg or home-made spirits can contain methanol: blurred vision, belly pain or breathlessness hours after drinking need urgent hospital care.
Children who swallow any adult medicine, opioid patch or alcohol need urgent medical care.
lessons.why: Opioids, alcohol and sleeping pills slow down the brain's breathing centre. The person gets too little oxygen, and without help the heart stops. Rescue breaths and CPR supply oxygen, and naloxone quickly blocks opioids, restarting breathing in many cases. Naloxone lasts less time than many opioids, so breathing can stop again, which is why you stay and still call. In alcohol poisoning, people often vomit while barely conscious and may choke, so the recovery position keeps their airway clear. Coffee, cold showers and sleep do not lower blood alcohol; they only give a false sense of safety.

quiz.q: You find a man unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, a needle nearby and very slow breathing. You have naloxone spray. What do you do?
options: Wait and see if he wakes
Call emergency services, give naloxone and support his breathing
Put him in a cold shower
quiz.why: This looks like an opioid overdose. Naloxone and breathing support save lives.

quiz.q: After naloxone he wakes up and wants to leave. Why should someone stay with him?
options: Naloxone can wear off and breathing can stop again
There is no need to stay
quiz.why: Many opioids last longer than naloxone. He needs monitoring and medical care.

quiz.q: A friend has drunk a lot, is barely awake and has vomited. What is best?
options: Lay him on his back to sleep
Put him in the recovery position, stay with him and call if he cannot be woken
quiz.why: Lying on the side keeps the airway clear if he vomits again.

sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025
AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
WHO guidelines on community management of opioid overdose

lessons.title: Panic attack
lessons.when: Sudden intense fear with fast breathing, pounding heart or tingling, once serious medical causes are unlikely.
recognize: Sudden intense fear or a sense of doom
Fast breathing, feeling unable to get enough air
Pounding heart, chest tightness, trembling, sweating
Tingling in hands, feet or around the mouth, dizziness
Usually peaks within about 10 minutes and then settles
steps: First ask yourself: could this be a heart attack, asthma, allergy or low sugar? If unsure, treat that.
Move them to a quieter place if you can, and stay with them.
Speak calmly and simply. Tell them they are safe and this will pass.
Breathe slowly with them: in through the nose, then a longer breath out through the mouth.
Help them focus on their surroundings, such as naming things they can see and hear.
Once settled, let them rest, give water and ask if this has happened before.
Suggest they see a doctor, especially if it is the first time or attacks keep happening.
dont: Do not make them breathe into a paper bag: it can lower oxygen levels.
Do not tell them to calm down or that it is all in their head.
Do not assume it is panic in someone with chest pain, diabetes, asthma, allergies or heart disease.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if there is chest pain, blue lips, collapse, confusion, a known heart or lung problem, it is their first attack, or symptoms do not settle within about 20 minutes.
special: Older people and anyone with heart risk factors: treat chest pain as a possible heart attack first.
Children: stay close, kneel to their level and breathe slowly together.
Pregnancy: breathlessness and a fast heart can have other causes; seek medical advice.
lessons.why: A panic attack is the body's alarm system firing when there is no real danger. Adrenaline speeds up the heart and breathing. Breathing too fast blows off carbon dioxide, which causes tingling, dizziness and chest tightness, and these feelings make the fear worse. Slow breathing with a longer breath out calms the nervous system and lets the carbon dioxide level settle. A calm person nearby helps them feel safe. Paper bag breathing is no longer advised because it can starve the body of oxygen, which is dangerous if the real cause is a heart or lung problem. Panic is a diagnosis to make only once those causes are unlikely.

quiz.q: A young woman with no medical history is breathing fast, shaking and says her fingers tingle after an argument. She is alert and has no chest pain. What helps most?
options: Calm reassurance and slow breathing with a long breath out
Leaving her alone to calm down
quiz.why: Slow breathing and calm company settle a panic attack safely.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old man says he is having a panic attack, with chest tightness and sweating. What do you do?
options: Treat as panic and do breathing exercises only
Treat as a possible heart attack and call emergency services
Tell him to walk it off
quiz.why: In older people or with chest pain, rule out a heart attack first.

quiz.q: Why is paper bag breathing no longer advised?
options: It can lower oxygen, which is dangerous if the cause is medical
quiz.why: Rebreathing can reduce oxygen, harmful if the cause is actually a heart or lung problem.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Head injury and concussion
lessons.when: Someone has hit their head, from a fall, a blow, a sports knock or a crash.
recognize: Bump, cut or bruise on the head or face
Headache, dizziness or feeling dazed
Confusion, memory gaps or repeating questions
Nausea or vomiting
Blurred vision or sensitivity to light or noise
Brief knockout, or drowsiness afterwards
steps: Check the scene is safe, then check if they respond and are breathing normally.
If unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) and start CPR.
If the fall or blow was hard, assume a neck injury: ask them to keep still.
Press a clean cloth on any scalp bleeding; scalps bleed a lot but usually stop with firm pressure.
Hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth on the bump for up to 20 minutes.
Check for red flags now and over the next 24 hours: worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, drowsiness, seizure.
Stop sport or activity for the day, even if they feel fine.
Keep someone with them for the first 24 hours and get them checked by a doctor.
dont: Do not let them return to sport, driving or diving the same day.
Do not leave them alone or let them drink alcohol after a head knock.
Do not move them if a neck injury is possible, unless they are in danger.
Do not press hard on a wound where the skull feels soft or dented.
lessons.call: Call at once if they were knocked out, are confused or drowsy, vomit more than once, have a seizure, weakness, slurred speech, unequal pupils, clear fluid or blood from the nose or ears, or take blood thinners. Anyone with concussion symptoms should see a doctor the same day.
special: Children: watch for unusual crying, not feeding, irritability or drowsiness; a baby with a head knock needs a doctor.
Elderly people and anyone on blood thinners can bleed inside the skull slowly: get them checked even after a minor knock.
Concussion: rest for a day or two, then return to school, work and sport step by step, and only once symptom free with a doctor's approval.
lessons.why: The brain is soft and floats inside a hard skull. A blow can shake it (concussion) or tear blood vessels so blood collects and presses on the brain. That pressure can build up over hours, which is why someone can seem fine and then get worse. The red flags are the signs of rising pressure or serious damage and need hospital care fast. A second knock before the brain has healed can cause much worse injury, so no return to sport the same day and a gradual return later. Hard falls and crashes can also injure the neck, so keeping still protects the spinal cord. Cold reduces swelling and pain.

quiz.q: A friend falls off a scooter, hits his head, seems fine, then two hours later is vomiting for the second time and getting sleepy. What do you do?
options: Wait until morning and see a doctor
quiz.why: Repeated vomiting and growing drowsiness are red flags for bleeding or swelling in the brain. This needs hospital care urgently.

quiz.q: A teenager takes a hard knock in basketball, feels dazed for a minute, then says he is fine and wants to play on. What is right?
options: Let him play if he can walk straight
Stop him playing for the rest of the day and get him checked
Let him play after 15 minutes rest
Only stop him if he was knocked out
quiz.why: Any concussion symptom means no more sport that day. A second knock while the brain is healing can be very dangerous.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old on blood thinners bumps her head on a cupboard. She has a small bruise and no other symptoms. What should happen?
options: Get her checked by a doctor today
quiz.why: Blood thinners and older age raise the risk of slow bleeding inside the skull, so even a minor knock needs a medical check.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
International Consensus on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam 2022)

lessons.title: Neck or back injury
lessons.when: After a fall from height, a diving accident, a crash or a heavy blow, when the neck or back could be hurt.
recognize: Neck or back pain after a fall, crash, dive or blow
Numbness, tingling or weakness in arms or legs
Cannot move arms or legs, or loss of bladder control
Head held at an odd angle
Head injury or unresponsive after a hard impact
steps: Make sure the scene is safe; do not move them unless they are in danger, such as traffic, fire or water.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Tell them to keep still and not nod or turn their head; answer questions by speaking.
Kneel behind their head and gently hold it in the position you found it, if you can.
Keep them warm and reassure them while you wait.
If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR at once: breathing comes before the spine.
If unresponsive but breathing, and they vomit or you must leave, roll them onto their side, keeping head and body in line.
Keep checking their breathing until help arrives.
dont: Do not move or pull them up to sitting or standing.
Do not twist the head to straighten it if it hurts or they resist.
Do not put a homemade collar on the neck.
Do not delay CPR because you are worried about the spine.
lessons.call: Always call emergency services for a suspected neck or back injury, especially with numbness, weakness, or after a dive, high fall or crash.
special: Diving in shallow water: if they are face down, support head and back together and turn them face up in the water, then keep them floating until help comes.
Elderly people can break their neck even in a simple fall from standing.
lessons.why: The spinal cord runs inside the bones of the neck and back. If a bone is broken, moving the person could press on the cord and cause permanent paralysis. Most people with a real injury hold themselves still because it hurts, so the safest thing is to ask them to keep still and wait for trained help with proper equipment. Guidelines no longer recommend collars from first aiders, as they can do harm. Gently holding the head is a reminder to keep still, not force. But a person who is not breathing will die within minutes, so CPR or protecting the airway always comes first, even if the spine might be hurt.

quiz.q: A man dives into a shallow river and is floating face down. Friends pull him to the bank. He is not breathing. What first?
options: Hold his neck still and wait for an ambulance
Turn him on his side and wait
quiz.why: Not breathing is the immediate threat to life. CPR comes first, even with a possible neck injury.

quiz.q: A woman fell from a ladder, is awake, and says her neck hurts and her hands tingle. She wants to stand up. What do you say?
options: Stay still, lie as you are, help is coming
Turn your head to see if it hurts
quiz.why: Neck pain with tingling suggests a spinal injury. Keeping still protects the spinal cord until professionals arrive.

quiz.q: A crash victim is lying on a busy road with a possible back injury, and traffic cannot be stopped. What should you do?
options: Leave him exactly where he is
Move him carefully off the road, keeping his body in line
Lift him by the arms quickly
Wait for the ambulance to move him
quiz.why: Danger to life overrides spinal concern. Move him only as far as needed, keeping head, neck and body in line.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Broken bone
lessons.when: A limb is painful, swollen or misshapen after a fall, crash or blow and a bone could be broken.
recognize: Severe pain, worse when moving
Swelling or bruising
Limb bent, shortened or at an odd angle
Cannot use or put weight on it
A grating feeling or a snap was heard
Bone visible through the skin (open fracture)
steps: Ask them to keep still and support the injured part in the position you found it.
If bone is through the skin, press around it, not on it, and cover with a clean dressing.
Splint only if you must move them: pad it, and fix the joints above and below the break.
Improvise: rolled magazine, cardboard, board or umbrella for a splint; a shirt, scarf or cloth as ties.
For an arm, make a sling from a triangular bandage, scarf or shirt; a leg can be tied to the good leg.
Check fingers or toes are warm, pink and can feel; loosen ties if they go numb, pale or blue.
Hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth on it for up to 20 minutes to ease pain and swelling.
Get them to hospital, or call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for a big or open break.
dont: Do not try to straighten a bent limb or push a bone back in.
Do not let them eat or drink if they may need surgery.
Do not tie splints so tight they cut off blood flow.
Do not move them unless there is danger or you have to.
lessons.call: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for a broken thigh, hip or pelvis, an open fracture, heavy bleeding, a limb that is cold, pale or numb below the injury, or signs of shock.
special: Children's bones can bend or crack without looking deformed: if a child will not use a limb, get an X-ray.
Elderly people who fall and cannot stand may have a broken hip: keep them warm and still and call for help.
lessons.why: Broken bone ends are sharp and can damage nearby blood vessels and nerves if they move. Keeping the limb still and supported reduces pain, bleeding and further damage. A splint works by stopping movement at the break and at the joints on either side, so the bone ends cannot shift. Padding avoids pressure sores. Straightening a limb without training can tear vessels, so leave that to professionals. Checking warmth and feeling below the injury tells you if blood is still reaching it. An open fracture can become badly infected, so it needs a clean cover and hospital care. Thigh and pelvis breaks can bleed a lot inside, causing shock.

quiz.q: A hiker's forearm is bent after a fall, 3 hours from a road. What do you do?
options: Pull it straight, then splint it
Splint it as found with padding, then make a sling
Leave it unsupported and walk out
Rub it to ease the pain
quiz.why: Splint in the position found, fixing the joints above and below, and support with a sling. Do not straighten it.

quiz.q: After you splint a lower leg, the toes turn pale and the person says they feel numb. What next?
options: Remove the splint completely and rub the leg
quiz.why: Pale, numb toes mean blood flow is reduced. Loosen the ties, recheck, and get help fast if it does not improve.

quiz.q: A bone is poking through the skin of a shin and bleeding. What is right?
options: Press firmly on the bone end
Press around the bone and cover with a clean dressing, then call
quiz.why: Control bleeding by pressing around the wound, cover it to reduce infection, and call. Never push bone back.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Sprain or strain
lessons.when: A twisted ankle, knee or wrist, or a pulled muscle, with pain and swelling but no obvious break.
recognize: Pain around a joint after twisting it
Swelling and bruising
Pain on moving or putting weight on it
Joint feels stiff or weak
steps: Stop the activity and rest the injured part.
Hold a cold pack or ice wrapped in a cloth on it for up to 20 minutes.
Repeat cooling every 2 to 3 hours during the first day or two.
Raise the limb above heart level when you can, to reduce swelling.
Support it with a firm but not tight bandage if that is more comfortable.
Use paracetamol for pain if they can take it, following the pack.
Start gentle movement after a day or two as the pain allows.
See a doctor if they cannot take four steps, or pain is on the bone itself.
dont: Do not put ice straight on bare skin.
Do not wrap a bandage so tight that fingers or toes go numb, pale or cold.
Do not keep playing or walking on it through the pain.
Do not massage or heat it in the first day or two.
lessons.call: See a doctor if they cannot bear weight, the joint is misshapen, there is pain right on the bone, numbness, or no improvement after a few days. A break can look like a sprain.
special: Children and elderly people are more likely to break a bone than sprain it: if in doubt, get an X-ray.
lessons.why: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament, the tough band that holds a joint together. A strain is a stretched muscle. Bleeding and fluid leak into the area, causing swelling and pain. Cold reduces pain and may limit swelling; wrapping ice in cloth prevents cold burns. Raising the limb helps fluid drain back. Resting at first lets healing start, but gentle movement after a day or two helps recovery and stops stiffness. Some sprains hide a broken bone, so being unable to walk, or pain pressing on the bone, means it needs an X-ray.

quiz.q: You roll your ankle on a trail. It swells but you can walk. What is best first?
options: Walk it off for another hour
Rest, cold pack wrapped in cloth for up to 20 minutes, raise it
quiz.why: Rest, cold wrapped in cloth and raising the leg ease pain and swelling. Heat and massage are for later.

quiz.q: After a twisted ankle, she cannot take four steps and the bony knob on the outside is very tender. What now?
options: Treat at home as a sprain
Get an X-ray, it may be broken
Strap it tight and keep going
quiz.why: Not being able to bear weight and bone tenderness suggest a fracture, which needs an X-ray.

quiz.q: You have no cold pack. What is a safe option?
options: Ice cubes straight on the skin
A bag of frozen vegetables or a cold drink can wrapped in a cloth
Nothing works without a proper ice pack
quiz.why: Anything cold wrapped in cloth works. A cloth prevents cold injury to the skin.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Dislocated joint
lessons.when: A joint such as a shoulder, finger, elbow or kneecap has popped out of place.
recognize: Joint looks out of shape or has a lump or dip
Severe pain and cannot move the joint
Swelling and bruising
Numbness or tingling below the joint
steps: Ask them to keep still and hold the joint in the most comfortable position.
Support it as found with pillows, rolled clothing or a sling.
Hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth on it for up to 20 minutes.
Check fingers or toes for warmth, colour and feeling.
Remove rings or watches from that hand before it swells.
Get them to hospital; call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if the hand or foot is cold, pale or numb.
Give nothing to eat or drink, in case they need sedation to fix it.
dont: Do not try to push or pull the joint back in.
Do not let them use the limb.
Do not move them more than needed.
lessons.call: Go to hospital for every dislocation. Call emergency services if the limb below is cold, pale, blue or numb, if a hip or knee is involved, or if there are other serious injuries.
special: Children: a pulled elbow in toddlers (refusing to use the arm after being swung or pulled) needs a doctor, not home treatment.
lessons.why: In a dislocation the bones of a joint are forced out of place, which stretches ligaments, nerves and blood vessels around it. There may also be a broken bone that you cannot see. Pushing it back without an X-ray, training and pain relief can trap nerves, tear vessels or worsen a fracture. Supporting the joint in the position they find most comfortable reduces pain and stops further damage. Cold eases pain and swelling. Checking feeling and colour below tells you if nerves and blood flow are compromised, which turns it into an emergency. Fasting helps because doctors often sedate the person to put the joint back.

quiz.q: A friend's shoulder pops out while swimming. He asks you to yank it back in like in the movies. What do you do?
options: Support the arm in a comfortable position and go to hospital
Let him swim back with it
Rub it until it goes back
quiz.why: Support it as found and get medical care. Pulling it in can damage nerves and vessels or worsen a hidden fracture.

quiz.q: After a dislocated elbow, the hand is cold and pale. What does that mean?
options: Blood flow may be blocked: call emergency services
quiz.why: A cold, pale hand means poor circulation. That needs urgent emergency care to save the limb.

quiz.q: Before going to hospital with a dislocated finger, what is wise?
options: Take off rings on that hand
quiz.why: Swelling can trap a ring and cut off blood flow, so remove rings early.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Burns
lessons.when: Skin burned by heat: fire, hot liquid, steam, hot metal such as a motorbike exhaust, or the sun.
recognize: Red, painful skin
Blisters
White, brown, black or leathery skin that may not hurt (deep burn)
Swelling
Soot around the mouth or nose, hoarse voice or cough (airway burn)
steps: Stop the burning: move away from the heat; if clothes are on fire, stop, drop and roll.
Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, starting as soon as possible.
While cooling, remove rings, watches and clothing near the burn, unless stuck to the skin.
Keep the rest of the person warm so they do not get too cold.
Cover loosely with cling film laid on in strips, or a clean non-fluffy cloth or dressing.
Give paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain if they can take it.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for large, deep or airway burns; keep cooling while you wait.
dont: Do not use ice, butter, oil, toothpaste or other home remedies.
Do not burst blisters or peel off skin.
Do not pull off clothing stuck to the burn.
Do not wrap cling film tightly around a limb.
Do not use fluffy cotton wool or sticky plasters on the burn.
lessons.call: Call emergency services for burns that are large (bigger than the person's palm), deep, on the face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, go all round a limb, or involve smoke or hot air breathed in. Children, elderly people and anyone unwell need a doctor for any burn bigger than a coin.
special: Children and infants cool fast: cool only the burn and keep the rest of the body warm and covered.
Elderly people have thin skin that burns deeply, so get even small burns checked.
If running water is not available, any cool clean water works; cooling helps even up to 3 hours after the burn.
lessons.why: Burned skin keeps cooking after the heat source is gone. Cooling with water for a full 20 minutes stops that, reduces pain, and lowers the chance of deep burns and scarring. Ice is too cold and damages tissue further, and greasy remedies trap heat and cause infection. Burned areas swell, so rings and watches come off early before they cut off blood flow. Cling film is clean, does not stick, and keeps air off the burn, which eases pain; laying it in strips avoids squeezing a swelling limb. Large burns make the body lose heat and fluid quickly, so keep the person warm and get help. Smoke can swell the airway within hours.

quiz.q: Your friend burns her calf on a hot motorbike exhaust. What first?
options: Hold it under cool running water for 20 minutes
quiz.why: Cool running water for 20 minutes is the most effective first aid for a burn. Ice and home remedies cause more harm.

quiz.q: A child pulls a cup of hot coffee onto his chest. While you cool it with water, what else should you do?
options: Pull off his shirt even where it sticks
Remove clothing that is not stuck, and keep the rest of him warm
Pop the blisters to let fluid out
Stop cooling after 2 minutes so he does not get cold
quiz.why: Remove clothing that is not stuck, cool the burn for 20 minutes, and keep the rest of the child warm. A chest burn this size in a child needs a doctor.

quiz.q: After a kitchen fire, a man has soot around his nose and a hoarse voice, but only small burns. What do you do?
options: Treat the small burns and send him home
Call emergency services, his airway may swell
Wait to see if his voice gets better
quiz.why: Soot and a hoarse voice suggest an airway burn, which can swell and block breathing. Call at once.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Chemical burn and splash
lessons.when: A chemical such as bleach, drain cleaner, battery acid, cement, pesticide or pool chemicals gets on the skin or in the eyes.
recognize: Stinging, burning pain where the chemical touched
Redness, blisters or grey or dark skin
Wet cement or lime on the skin for a long time
Eye pain, watering, redness, or trouble opening the eye
Blurred vision
steps: Protect yourself: wear gloves if you can, and move away from fumes into fresh air.
Brush off dry powder first, such as lime or cement, before adding water.
Remove contaminated clothing, jewellery and watches, taking care not to spread the chemical.
Flush skin with lots of running water for at least 20 minutes, letting water run off, not onto other skin.
For eyes: hold the eyelids open and pour water from the inner corner outward, away from the other eye.
Remove contact lenses if they come out easily, then keep flushing.
Find the container or name of the chemical and call a poison centre or call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Keep flushing until help arrives or the pain stops, then cover the skin loosely.
dont: Do not try to neutralise acid with alkali or the other way round: it makes heat.
Do not rub the eye or the skin.
Do not stop flushing early because the pain eases.
Do not wet dry powder before brushing it off.
lessons.call: Go to hospital for every chemical splash in the eye, and for any chemical burn that is large, deep, on the face, hands or genitals. Call emergency services if they have trouble breathing, swallowed the chemical, or feel faint.
special: Children: if a child has swallowed a chemical, do not make them vomit; call a poison centre or emergency services.
For an infant's eye, lay them on their back, hold the eyelids open, and pour gently from a cup.
lessons.why: A chemical keeps burning until it is removed or diluted, sometimes for a long time. Lots of water washes it away and cools the skin. Strong alkalis such as drain cleaner, cement and lime soak deep and are especially dangerous to the eye, so flushing longer is better. Dry powder can react with water, so brushing it off first is safer. Trying to neutralise a chemical with another chemical creates heat and more damage. Flushing from the inner corner of the eye outward stops the chemical washing into the other eye. Protecting yourself first avoids a second casualty. The chemical's name helps doctors and poison experts choose treatment.

quiz.q: A builder's forearm is covered in dry lime powder and burning. What first?
options: Brush off the dry powder, then flush with lots of water
Rub vinegar on it to neutralise it
quiz.why: Brush off dry chemical first, then flush with plenty of running water. Never try to neutralise it.

quiz.q: Bleach splashes in a child's eye. How do you flush it?
options: Have her blink a few times
Hold the eye open and pour water from the inner corner outward for at least 20 minutes
Put eye drops in and wait
quiz.why: Flush for a long time with the eye held open, pouring away from the other eye, then go to hospital.

quiz.q: After 5 minutes of flushing, the pain is gone. Should you stop?
options: No, keep flushing for at least 20 minutes
quiz.why: Chemicals can keep damaging tissue after pain eases. Keep flushing for the full time.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Electric shock and lightning
lessons.when: Someone has touched a live wire, appliance or fallen power line, or has been struck by lightning.
recognize: Person still touching a cable, appliance or wet area
Unresponsive or not breathing normally
Burns where current went in and out, often hands and feet
Muscle pain, confusion, or irregular heartbeat
Thrown or fallen, with other injuries
steps: Do not touch them until the power is off: switch off at the mains, unplug, or remove the fuse.
For high voltage or fallen power lines, stay far back, at least 18 metres, until the power company cuts it.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Once safe, if they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and send for an AED.
If breathing but unresponsive, put them in the recovery position and keep checking breathing.
Cool burns under cool running water for 20 minutes and cover loosely with cling film or a clean dressing.
Lightning: a struck person carries no charge; touch and help them at once, while staying safe from further strikes.
Lightning with several casualties: help those who look dead first, as CPR often saves them.
dont: Do not touch the person, or water around them, while the current may be live.
Do not use a wet or metal object to push a cable away; dry wood or plastic only, for low voltage.
Do not shelter under a lone tree or stay in open water during lightning.
Do not skip a medical check because they seem fine.
lessons.call: Call emergency services for any high voltage shock, lightning strike, unresponsiveness, breathing problems, burns, or chest pain. Everyone who has had an electric shock should be checked by a doctor, as the heart rhythm can be affected.
special: Children who bite cables can get burns at the corner of the mouth that bleed days later: see a doctor.
Pregnant women should always be checked after a shock, even a small one, as it can affect the baby.
lessons.why: Electricity flows through the body and can stop the heart or breathing, and burns tissue on its way. If you touch someone still connected, it flows through you too, so cutting the power comes first. High voltage can jump through the air and the ground, which is why you stay far away. A person struck by lightning does not hold any charge, so they are safe to touch. Lightning often stops the heart and breathing, but the heart may restart with prompt CPR, so those who look dead are helped first. Burns on the skin can hide deeper damage, so anyone shocked needs a check, even if they feel fine.

quiz.q: A woman collapses while holding a frayed fan cable. What first?
options: Grab her arm and pull her away
Switch off or unplug at the wall first
Start CPR straight away while she holds the cable
quiz.why: Cut the power before touching her, or the current can pass into you.

quiz.q: Lightning strikes near a beach group. One person is groaning with burns, another lies silent and not breathing. Who first?
options: The silent person who is not breathing: start CPR
Neither, wait for the storm to pass
Whoever is closest to the water
quiz.why: With lightning, people who look dead often recover with quick CPR. Those groaning are breathing.

quiz.q: A man got a small shock from a socket and feels fine. What is best?
options: Get a medical check, as the heart rhythm can be affected
quiz.why: Electricity can disturb the heart rhythm and cause hidden injuries, so a medical check is wise.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)
ERC Guidelines 2021: Cardiac arrest in special circumstances

lessons.title: Eye injury
lessons.when: Something is in the eye, the eye has been hit, or it has been cut or pierced.
recognize: Pain, watering, redness or a gritty feeling
Cannot open the eye or bright light hurts
Blurred, double or lost vision
Blood in the white or coloured part of the eye
Cut on the eye or eyelid, or an object stuck in the eye
steps: Wash your hands and ask them not to rub the eye.
Speck of dust or sand: let them blink, then flush with clean water from the inner corner outward.
If the speck stays, gently lift it off the white of the eye with a wet clean cloth corner.
Object stuck in the eye: leave it; cover with a paper cup taped in place, without touching the object.
Blow to the eye: hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth lightly on it for up to 15 minutes, no pressure.
Cut eye: cover loosely with a clean dressing and do not press on the eyeball.
Ask them to keep both eyes still; covering the good eye too can stop the injured eye moving.
Chemical in the eye: flush with water for at least 20 minutes and see the chemical burn lesson.
dont: Do not rub the eye.
Do not try to remove anything stuck into the eye or on the coloured part.
Do not press on an injured eyeball.
Do not use tweezers or anything sharp near the eye.
lessons.call: Go to hospital urgently for any object stuck in the eye, a cut eye, changes in vision, blood inside the eye, a high speed fragment from grinding or hammering, or pain that does not settle. Call emergency services if the eye is pierced.
special: Children may not keep still or say their vision has changed: take any eye injury in a child to a doctor.
Contact lens wearers: remove lenses before flushing if possible, and see a doctor if pain continues.
lessons.why: The eye is delicate and can be permanently damaged. Rubbing drags grit across the clear front layer and scratches it. Water flushes out loose specks gently; flushing from the inner corner stops dirt washing into the other eye. An object stuck in the eye may be plugging a hole, so removing it or pressing on the eye can push the contents out. A paper cup protects it without pressure. Both eyes move together, so keeping both still, or covering both, reduces movement of the injured one. Cold lightly applied eases swelling after a blow. Fast metal fragments from grinding can enter the eye with little pain, so they always need a check.

quiz.q: Sand blows into your friend's eye at the beach. What first?
options: Let her blink, then flush with clean water
Lick a cloth and wipe the coloured part
quiz.why: Blinking and gentle flushing with clean water usually wash out loose specks. Rubbing can scratch the eye.

quiz.q: A splinter of wood is stuck in a man's eye after chopping. What do you do?
options: Cover the eye with a paper cup without touching the splinter and go to hospital
Press a pad firmly on the eye
Flush hard to wash it out
quiz.why: Never remove an object stuck in the eye. Protect it without pressure and get urgent help.

quiz.q: After being hit by a ball, a girl says her vision is blurry. What does that mean?
options: It is normal, it will pass
She needs an eye doctor today
quiz.why: Any change in vision after a blow can mean serious damage inside the eye and needs urgent care.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Knocked-out tooth
lessons.when: A permanent (adult) tooth has been knocked out by a fall, blow or crash.
recognize: A whole tooth is out of the socket
Bleeding from the gum
Pain in the mouth or jaw
Other teeth loose or broken
steps: Find the tooth and hold it only by the crown, the white part you chew with, never the root.
If dirty, rinse it briefly in milk, saline or cold running water, for no more than about 10 seconds.
If they are alert and it is an adult tooth, push it gently back into its socket, the right way round.
Ask them to bite on a clean cloth to hold the tooth in place.
If you cannot put it back, keep it in milk, saline or coconut water, or wrapped in cling film.
Press a clean cloth on the gum to stop bleeding.
Get to a dentist or emergency department as fast as possible, ideally within 30 minutes.
dont: Do not touch or scrub the root.
Do not let the tooth dry out.
Do not store it in plain water.
Do not put a baby tooth back in.
lessons.call: See a dentist at once for a knocked-out adult tooth. Call emergency services if there is a head injury, heavy bleeding, or breathing problems, or if the tooth may have been inhaled.
special: Children: baby teeth are not put back, as this can harm the adult tooth growing underneath, but still see a dentist.
Do not ask a young child to keep the tooth in their mouth, as they may swallow or inhale it.
lessons.why: The root of a tooth is covered with living cells that help it reattach to the bone. Those cells die quickly if the tooth dries out or the root is touched or scrubbed. Putting the tooth back straight away gives the best chance of saving it, because the socket is the ideal place to keep the cells alive. If that is not possible, milk, saline or coconut water keep the cells alive much better than water, which makes them swell and burst. Speed matters most: a tooth replanted within minutes often survives, while one left dry for an hour usually does not. A dentist will splint it in place.

quiz.q: A teenager's front tooth is knocked out in a game. It is clean. What is best?
options: Wrap it in a dry tissue
Hold it by the crown and push it back into the socket, then see a dentist
Put it in a glass of water
quiz.why: Replanting at once gives the best chance of saving an adult tooth. Hold it only by the crown.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old knocks out a baby tooth. Should you put it back?
options: No, baby teeth are not replanted, but see a dentist
quiz.why: Replanting a baby tooth can damage the adult tooth underneath.

quiz.q: You cannot replant the tooth. Which is the best thing to carry it in?
quiz.why: Milk, saline or coconut water keep root cells alive. Water and drying kill them.

lessons.title: Road and motorbike crash
lessons.when: You arrive at a road crash, such as a motorbike or tricycle collision, with one or more people hurt.
recognize: Vehicles crashed, riders on the ground
Traffic still moving around the scene
Fuel leaking, smoke or fire
People unresponsive, bleeding, or trapped
Rider still wearing a helmet
steps: Stop safely away from the crash, hazard lights on; get bystanders to warn and slow traffic from both directions.
Turn off engines, no smoking, and stay clear of fuel leaks or fire.
Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines): say how many are hurt and the exact location.
Many casualties: check silent, still ones first; people shouting or walking are breathing.
For each: stop heavy bleeding with firm pressure, and start CPR if not breathing normally.
Leave the helmet on; open the visor to check breathing, and remove it only if the airway needs it.
To remove a helmet, use two people: one holds the head and neck still, the other eases the helmet off.
Do not move injured people unless they are in danger; ask them to keep still and keep them warm.
Cool any exhaust burns with water and stay with them until help arrives.
dont: Do not run into moving traffic.
Do not pull a rider up to sitting or standing.
Do not remove a helmet if they are breathing well and you can reach the airway.
Do not give food or drink.
Do not spend time on minor injuries while others may be dying.
lessons.call: Call emergency services for any crash with injuries, people trapped or unresponsive, motorbike riders thrown off, fire, or fuel leaks. If no ambulance can come, organise safe transport to the nearest hospital.
special: Children in a crash can hide serious injuries: get every child checked at hospital.
Pregnant women should always go to hospital after a crash, even if they feel fine.
lessons.why: At a crash, traffic and fire can quickly make more victims, so making the scene safe comes first. When there are many casualties, the quiet ones are the most likely to have a blocked airway or not be breathing, while people shouting are at least breathing. Stopping heavy bleeding and starting CPR save the most lives. Motorbike riders often have head and neck injuries, so a helmet is left on to avoid moving the neck, unless it stops you opening the airway or giving CPR. Then two people remove it, keeping the head and neck in line. Exhaust pipe burns are very common and need cooling like any burn.

quiz.q: A motorbike rider lies on the road, breathing normally, wearing a full face helmet. What do you do with the helmet?
options: Take it off so he can breathe better
Leave it on, open the visor and watch his breathing
Remove it to check for cuts
quiz.why: If breathing well, leave the helmet on to protect the neck. Remove it only if the airway or CPR needs it.

quiz.q: Three people are hurt in a tricycle crash. One is screaming, one is walking around, one is silent and still. Who do you check first?
quiz.why: A silent, still person may not be breathing. Screaming and walking mean breathing is working.

quiz.q: You stop at a crash on a dark highway. What is your very first priority?
options: Make the scene safe: park safely, hazard lights, warn traffic
quiz.why: Without scene safety, you or others can be hit. Make it safe, then help the injured.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke
lessons.when: Someone is unwell after heat, sun or hard exercise: weak, dizzy, vomiting, confused or collapsed.
recognize: Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, pale or flushed clammy skin, weakness, dizziness
Heat exhaustion: headache, nausea, thirst, muscle cramps, fast pulse
Heat stroke: confusion, odd behaviour, slurred speech or stumbling
Heat stroke: seizure, collapse or not responding normally
Heat stroke: very hot skin, which may be dry or still sweaty
Any change in thinking or behaviour in the heat means heat stroke until proven otherwise
steps: If they are confused, collapsed or acting strangely, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) now: treat it as heat stroke.
Move them out of the sun into shade or a cool room, and stop all activity.
Heat stroke: cool them fast, ideally in cold water up to the neck, with someone holding their head above water.
If you cannot immerse them, soak them with cold water and fan hard; add ice packs to neck, armpits and groin.
Keep cooling until they think clearly again or help takes over; do not wait for an ambulance to start.
Heat exhaustion: lie them down, raise their legs, loosen or remove extra clothing, and fan them.
If fully alert and not vomiting, give sips of cool water or an electrolyte or rehydration drink.
If they become confused or are not clearly better within about 30 minutes, treat it as heat stroke.
If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, start CPR.
dont: Do not give drinks to someone who is confused, drowsy or vomiting.
Do not give paracetamol or aspirin to bring the temperature down; they do not work for heat illness.
Do not delay cooling to wait for transport or a thermometer.
Do not let them go back to work or play the same day.
lessons.call: Call at once for any confusion, collapse, seizure or unresponsiveness. Get medical care for heat exhaustion that does not improve with rest, cooling and fluids.
special: Children, older people and people on some heart or mental health medicines overheat faster. Never leave a child in a parked car.
In pregnancy, heat illness also stresses the baby: cool and get checked early.
lessons.why: Your body cools itself mainly by sweating. In hot, humid places like the Philippines, sweat evaporates slowly, so heat builds up, especially during hard work or exercise. Heat exhaustion is the warning stage: the body is struggling but the brain still works. Heat stroke is when the core gets so hot that the brain and organs start to fail, shown by confusion or collapse. Damage depends on how hot and for how long, so the speed of cooling matters most. Cold water immersion pulls heat out faster than anything else, which is why it is the first choice. Fanning a wet body is the next best. Fever medicines do not help because heat stroke is not a fever: the body's thermostat is fine, it is simply overwhelmed.

quiz.q: After a midday hike, your friend is sweaty, pale and dizzy but talking normally. What first?
options: Move to shade, lie down with legs up, cool and give sips of water
Keep walking slowly to the car
Put them in a hot shower
quiz.why: This is heat exhaustion. Rest, cooling and fluids usually fix it; watch for confusion.

quiz.q: A runner collapses on a hot day and is confused about where she is. Which cooling is best?
options: Cold water immersion up to the neck while someone calls 911
Wait for the ambulance to cool her
quiz.why: Confusion means heat stroke. Rapid cold water immersion is the fastest way to bring the temperature down.

quiz.q: A worker with heat exhaustion has rested for 30 minutes but is now drowsy and muddled. What now?
options: Treat as heat stroke: call and cool aggressively
Give a large bottle of water to drink
quiz.why: Getting worse or new confusion means heat stroke. Do not give drinks to a drowsy person.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Dehydration and diarrhoea
lessons.when: Someone has diarrhoea, vomiting or has lost a lot of fluid through heat and sweat.
recognize: Thirst, dry mouth and lips, little or dark yellow urine
Tiredness, dizziness when standing, headache
Sunken eyes; in babies a sunken soft spot on the head and few wet nappies
Skin that goes back slowly when pinched
Severe: very drowsy or floppy, unable to drink, fast breathing, cold hands and feet
steps: Start oral rehydration salts (ORS) early: mix one packet with the exact amount of clean water printed on it.
No packet? Make WHO home ORS: 1 litre clean water, 6 level teaspoons sugar, half a level teaspoon salt.
Give small sips often: a teaspoon every minute or two for a child, more for adults, even if vomiting.
If they vomit, wait 10 minutes, then start again more slowly.
Give extra fluid after every loose stool; keep going until urine is pale and frequent.
Keep breastfeeding babies, and offer normal food as soon as they want to eat.
Wash hands with soap after the toilet and before food; use safe, boiled or treated water.
Take a child with diarrhoea to a health centre for ORS and zinc tablets, which WHO recommends for 10 to 14 days.
dont: Do not use soft drinks, sweet juice or sports drinks instead of ORS; too much sugar can worsen diarrhoea.
Do not add more salt or sugar than the recipe says; too much salt is dangerous, especially for babies.
Do not give anti-diarrhoea medicine such as loperamide to children.
Do not stop feeding or breastfeeding.
lessons.call: Go to hospital, or call emergency services (911 in the Philippines), for someone very drowsy, unable to drink or keep fluids down, with blood in the stool, high fever, no urine for many hours, or a baby under 6 months with diarrhoea.
special: Babies and young children dehydrate within hours; check wet nappies and seek care early.
Older people may not feel thirsty; offer drinks regularly.
Pregnant women with severe vomiting or diarrhoea should be seen by a doctor.
lessons.why: Diarrhoea and vomiting drain water and salts from the body, and losing them faster than you take them in is dangerous, especially for children. ORS works because the gut absorbs salt and sugar together, and water follows them in. That is why plain water is not enough and why the right balance matters: too much sugar draws water into the gut and worsens diarrhoea, and too much salt can harm the brain. Ready made low osmolarity ORS packets are best; the home recipe is a safe backup if measured carefully. Small, frequent sips are kept down better than big gulps. Zinc shortens diarrhoea in children. Most diarrhoea clears in a few days, but dehydration, not the germ, is what usually makes people seriously ill.

quiz.q: You have no ORS packets. How do you make WHO home ORS?
options: 1 litre water, 6 level teaspoons sugar, half a level teaspoon salt
1 litre cola with a pinch of salt
quiz.why: This is the WHO home recipe. Measure carefully: too much salt is dangerous.

quiz.q: A toddler with diarrhoea vomits after drinking ORS. What should you do?
options: Wait 10 minutes, then give small sips by teaspoon
quiz.why: Small frequent sips are usually kept down. Stopping fluids makes dehydration worse.

quiz.q: Which child needs hospital now?
options: Drinking well with mild tummy ache
Very drowsy, will not drink, no wet nappy for many hours
Asking for food after a day of diarrhoea
quiz.why: Drowsiness, refusing drinks and no urine are signs of severe dehydration.

sources: WHO: Treatment of diarrhoea, manual for physicians and other senior health workers
WHO/UNICEF guidance on ORS and zinc

lessons.title: Hypothermia (too cold)
lessons.when: Someone is very cold after time in water, rain, wind or at altitude, even in the tropics.
recognize: Shivering, pale cold skin, numb clumsy hands
Slurred speech, confusion, poor decisions, stumbling
Drowsiness or unusual quietness
Shivering that stops while they are still cold is a bad sign
Slow, shallow breathing and weak pulse in severe cases
steps: If they are drowsy, confused or not shivering despite being cold, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Move them gently out of the water, wind and rain into shelter. Handle them carefully and keep them lying flat.
Remove wet clothing gently, cutting it off if needed, and replace with dry clothes.
Insulate from the ground and wrap in blankets or sleeping bags, covering the head; add a plastic or foil layer.
Put wrapped warm packs or warm bottles against the chest, armpits and back, never directly on bare skin.
If fully alert and able to swallow, give warm sweet drinks and high energy food.
Check breathing often. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and keep going until help arrives.
dont: Do not rub or massage the arms and legs.
Do not put them in a hot bath or shower or use very hot water bottles on skin.
Do not give alcohol or let them smoke.
Do not let a severely cold person walk or exercise to warm up.
lessons.call: Call for anyone confused, drowsy, not shivering while cold, or unresponsive. Get medical care for anyone who was very cold, even if they recover.
special: Babies and older people lose heat quickly and may not shiver; feel the chest and tummy for coldness.
After a near drowning, people often get cold fast: keep them wrapped even on a warm beach.
lessons.why: When the core of the body cools, the brain slows down and the heart becomes irritable. A rough jolt or sudden movement can trigger a dangerous heart rhythm in a very cold person, which is why you handle them gently and keep them lying down. Wet clothes and wind pull heat away many times faster than dry air, so getting dry and out of the wind comes first. Insulation, including underneath them, stops further loss. Warmth on the chest and armpits warms the core. Rubbing limbs or a hot bath sends cold blood from the limbs back to the heart and can make things worse. Drinks only help if they are alert enough to swallow safely. Long CPR can still work in hypothermia.

quiz.q: A diver pulled from a long drift dive is shivering hard but talking sensibly. Best plan?
options: Get dry, wrap up including head, give a warm sweet drink
Make him jog to warm up
quiz.why: Mild hypothermia: dry, insulate and warm drinks while alert. No alcohol or exercise.

quiz.q: A cold hiker has stopped shivering and is mumbling and drowsy. What does this mean?
options: Severe hypothermia: call, handle gently, keep flat and insulate
quiz.why: Shivering stopping while still cold and drowsiness signal severe hypothermia.

quiz.q: Where should you place warm packs?
options: Wrapped, against the chest, armpits and back
Directly on bare hands and feet
quiz.why: Warming the core is safest. Wrap packs to avoid burns on numb skin.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Animal bites and rabies
lessons.when: Bitten, scratched or licked on broken skin by a dog, cat, monkey, bat or other mammal.
recognize: Bite or scratch that breaks the skin, even a tiny one
Lick on broken skin or saliva in the eyes, nose or mouth
Any bat contact, even without a visible wound
Bleeding, puncture marks, torn skin
Later: redness, swelling, warmth or pus means infection
steps: Get away from the animal safely. Control heavy bleeding with firm pressure first.
Wash the wound at once with soap and running water for 15 minutes. Start the timer.
Then apply povidone iodine or alcohol if you have it, and cover loosely with a clean dressing.
Go the same day to an Animal Bite Treatment Centre or hospital for rabies post exposure care.
Tell them the animal, the place, and whether it was owned, vaccinated, sick or acting strangely.
Complete every dose of the rabies vaccine schedule you are given, on the dates given.
Ask about tetanus and antibiotics. For a macaque monkey bite, ask about herpes B virus too.
If the dog or cat can be watched safely, ask the owner to report if it sickens or dies within 10 days.
dont: Do not wait to see if the animal gets sick before seeking care.
Do not rely on traditional healers or rubbing garlic, chilli or other substances into the wound.
Do not skip care because the wound is small or the animal looked healthy.
Do not try to catch or kill the animal yourself.
lessons.call: Seek rabies care the same day for any bite, scratch or lick on broken skin. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for heavy bleeding, a deep bite to the face, neck or hands, or severe injury.
special: Children are bitten more often, on the face and head, and may not tell you; ask about any contact with animals.
Rabies vaccine is safe in pregnancy and for babies; never delay it for these reasons.
If you were vaccinated before, you still need booster doses after a bite.
lessons.why: Rabies is spread in saliva and is common in dogs in the Philippines and much of Asia. Once symptoms start it is almost always fatal, but care given promptly after a bite prevents it reliably. Washing for 15 minutes with soap and running water physically removes and kills much of the virus and is one of the most important steps. Post exposure care means a course of rabies vaccine and, for deeper bites, rabies immunoglobulin into the wound, which neutralises virus before the vaccine takes effect. That is why speed matters and why you go even if the animal looks well. Animal mouths also carry bacteria, so bites often get infected. Macaques can carry herpes B virus, which is rare but serious.

quiz.q: A stray puppy nips your hand and draws a little blood. It looks healthy. What do you do?
options: Nothing, it is just a puppy
Wash 15 minutes with soap and running water, then go to an Animal Bite Treatment Centre today
Wait 10 days and see if the puppy dies
Put a plaster on and forget it
quiz.why: Any bite that breaks the skin needs washing and same day rabies assessment, whatever the animal looks like.

quiz.q: How long should you wash a bite wound?
options: 15 minutes with soap and running water
quiz.why: Prolonged washing with soap and water is a key part of rabies prevention.

quiz.q: A monkey at a temple scratches your child's arm. What is correct?
options: Wash well and get same day rabies care, and mention it was a monkey
Only see a doctor if a fever starts
quiz.why: Monkeys can transmit rabies, and macaques can carry herpes B; tell the clinic.

sources: WHO Expert Consultation on Rabies, third report (2018)
WHO position paper on rabies vaccines (2018)
Philippine Department of Health rabies programme

lessons.title: Snakebite
lessons.when: Someone has been bitten, or may have been bitten, by a snake, including a sea snake.
recognize: One or two puncture marks, sometimes just scratches or nothing visible
Pain, swelling, bruising or blistering spreading from the bite
Bleeding from gums, nose or the bite; blood in urine
Drooping eyelids, double vision, trouble swallowing, talking or breathing
Nausea, vomiting, sweating, dizziness or collapse
Spitting cobra venom in the eyes: severe pain and redness
steps: Move away from the snake. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) and arrange fast transport to a hospital that has antivenom.
Keep the person calm, lying still, and do not let them walk if they can be carried.
Remove rings, watches, bracelets and tight clothing from the bitten limb before it swells.
Keep the bitten limb still with a splint or sling, roughly at heart level.
Note the time of the bite and photograph the snake only if it is safe; never try to catch it.
For paralysis risk (cobra, krait, sea snake), a firm wide bandage up the whole limb plus splint may help; see notes.
For venom in the eyes, rinse immediately with lots of clean water for at least 10 to 15 minutes.
Give paracetamol for pain if needed. Be ready to give rescue breaths or CPR if breathing fails.
dont: Do not use a tourniquet or a tight cord around the limb.
Do not cut, suck, burn or apply ice, chemicals, herbs or electric shock to the bite.
Do not give aspirin or ibuprofen, which can worsen bleeding.
Do not wait for symptoms before going to hospital; some bites look harmless for hours.
Do not rely on a traditional healer; it delays antivenom.
lessons.call: Every snakebite needs hospital assessment, even if it seems minor. Call immediately for any breathing difficulty, drooping eyelids, bleeding or collapse.
special: Children get a larger dose of venom for their size and become ill faster; get them to hospital urgently.
In pregnancy, venom can harm the baby; treat it as an emergency and tell the hospital she is pregnant.
Pressure immobilisation is standard in Australia and for neurotoxic snakes such as cobras, kraits and sea snakes; WHO and others debate it, and it is not advised for viper bites with swelling.
lessons.why: Most snakes are not venomous, and many venomous bites inject little venom, but you cannot tell at the scene. Antivenom, given in hospital, is the only real treatment, so fast transport is the priority. Venom spreads mainly through the lymph channels, which are pumped by muscle movement. Keeping the person and the limb still slows the spread. Removing rings early prevents them cutting off the circulation when the limb swells. Tourniquets, cutting and sucking do not remove venom and cause serious extra harm such as lost limbs and infection. A pressure bandage can slow the spread of nerve toxins from cobras, kraits and sea snakes, but for vipers it may trap venom and worsen local damage, which is why advice differs.

quiz.q: Your friend is bitten on the ankle on a jungle trail. The snake has gone. What first?
options: Tie a tight tourniquet above the bite
Keep him still, splint the leg, call and carry him to hospital
quiz.why: Stillness and fast transport to antivenom are what help. Tourniquets and cutting cause harm.

quiz.q: A bitten man feels fine an hour later and wants to skip hospital. What do you say?
options: Go anyway: some venoms take hours to show effects
quiz.why: Symptoms such as paralysis or bleeding can be delayed. Hospital observation is needed.

quiz.q: A cobra spits into a farmer's eyes. What do you do?
options: Rinse the eyes with lots of clean water at once, then get medical care
Cover the eyes and do nothing
quiz.why: Immediate, prolonged rinsing removes venom and limits eye damage.

sources: WHO Guidelines for the management of snakebites (2nd edition, 2016)
AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Jellyfish stings
lessons.when: Stung by a jellyfish or touched by tentacles in the sea.
recognize: Sudden burning pain where tentacles touched
Red lines, whip marks or a ladder pattern on the skin
Box jellyfish: severe pain, collapse, trouble breathing, confusion
Delayed severe back or belly pain, sweating, vomiting and anxiety within an hour (Irukandji type)
Itching, rash or swelling with mild stings
steps: Get the person out of the water safely. Call for help from lifeguards.
If it may be a box jellyfish, or they have severe symptoms, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Box jellyfish: pour vinegar over the sting for at least 30 seconds before removing any tentacles.
Then lift off tentacles with tweezers, a card edge or gloved fingers, not bare hands.
If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, start CPR at once.
No vinegar? Rinse with plenty of seawater and remove tentacles carefully.
For pain, immerse or shower the area in hot water, as hot as is comfortable, about 45 C, for about 20 minutes.
If hot water is not available, use a cold pack wrapped in cloth.
dont: Do not rinse with fresh water before deactivating; it can make remaining stinging cells fire.
Do not rub the area or scrub with sand or a towel.
Do not use urine, alcohol or soft drinks.
Do not leave someone with a box jellyfish sting alone; collapse can happen within minutes.
lessons.call: Call for any suspected box jellyfish sting, large stings, breathing difficulty, chest pain, severe back pain, confusion or collapse. Stings to the eye or face also need medical care.
special: Children are at higher risk from box jellyfish because of their small size; call early.
For bluebottles (Portuguese man o' war), Australian guidance uses seawater rinse and hot water, not vinegar.
lessons.why: Jellyfish tentacles are covered with tiny stinging cells that fire venom when touched. Many cells stay loaded on the skin after the sting. For box jellyfish, vinegar stops the unfired cells from firing, which is why you use it before pulling off tentacles; removing them first can inject more venom. Box jellyfish live in Philippine and Thai waters and can stop the heart within minutes, so calling early and being ready for CPR matter most. Fresh water and rubbing can trigger the remaining cells. Hot water helps pain in many jellyfish stings because it is thought to break down the venom. Advice differs for bluebottles, where vinegar may cause more firing, so use seawater and hot water.

quiz.q: A child screams after swimming at dusk in Palawan and has ladder-like red marks on her leg. What first?
