options: Get her out, call, pour vinegar for at least 30 seconds, watch breathing
Pull tentacles off with bare hands immediately
quiz.why: This may be a box jellyfish. Vinegar first, then remove tentacles, and be ready for CPR.

quiz.q: Why pour vinegar before removing box jellyfish tentacles?
options: It stops unfired stinging cells from injecting more venom
It is an antidote to the venom in the blood
quiz.why: Vinegar deactivates the stinging cells on the skin. It does not treat venom already absorbed.

quiz.q: After a mild sting, with tentacles removed, what helps the pain most?
options: Hot water about 45 C for about 20 minutes
quiz.why: Hot water immersion, as hot as comfortable, is the recommended pain relief.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Stonefish, urchin, stingray, cone snail
lessons.when: Stung or spiked by a stonefish, lionfish, sea urchin, stingray or cone snail.
recognize: Stonefish or lionfish: intense pain right away, swelling, puncture wounds
Sea urchin: black or purple spines stuck in the skin
Stingray: deep cut or puncture, bleeding, severe pain, sometimes a barb left in
Cone snail: small sting, then numbness spreading, weakness, blurred vision, trouble breathing
Faintness, vomiting or breathing trouble in severe cases
steps: Get them out of the water. For breathing trouble, collapse, or chest or belly wounds, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Cone snail sting: keep them still, apply a firm bandage up the limb and splint it; be ready for rescue breaths.
Stingray barb in the chest, belly or neck: leave it in, keep them still and call.
Control bleeding with firm pressure, then rinse the wound with clean water.
Put the limb in hot water, as hot as tolerated, about 45 C, for at least 20 minutes or until pain eases.
Test the water with your own hand first; numb skin burns easily.
Lift out loose, visible spines with tweezers; do not dig for deep or broken ones.
Get the wound checked at a clinic for retained spines, infection, tetanus and stronger pain relief.
dont: Do not use hot water so hot that it burns; test it on unaffected skin.
Do not cut the wound or try to suck out venom.
Do not pull out a stingray barb from the chest, belly or neck.
Do not use urine or vinegar as treatment for these stings.
lessons.call: Call for any cone snail sting, breathing difficulty, collapse, or stingray wound to the chest, belly or neck. All stingray and stonefish wounds need medical care.
special: Children may need medical pain relief and are more affected by venom; seek care early.
Stonefish antivenom exists in some hospitals; severe stonefish pain or weakness needs hospital.
lessons.why: Stonefish, lionfish and stingray venoms are proteins that are broken down by heat, so hot water immersion is the best first aid for pain. The water must be hot enough to work but not burn, and the injured skin may not feel heat properly, so test it with your own hand. Stingray barbs cause deep wounds that can bleed, leave fragments and get badly infected, and a barb in the chest or belly can be fatal, so leave it for the hospital. Cone snail venom is different: it paralyses nerves and has no antivenom. Pressure and stillness slow its spread, and breathing support keeps the person alive until it wears off. Sea urchin spines often break; deep ones need a clinic.

quiz.q: You step on something on a reef and your foot is in agonising pain with puncture marks. What helps most?
options: Soak in hot water, about 45 C, tested first, then see a clinic
quiz.why: Likely stonefish or similar. Heat breaks down the venom and eases pain.

quiz.q: A snorkeller picked up a cone shell and now has numb lips and blurred vision. What do you do?
options: Call, keep still, pressure bandage the limb, be ready for rescue breaths
quiz.why: Cone snail venom can paralyse breathing. Breathing support is lifesaving.

quiz.q: A stingray barb is lodged in a swimmer's chest. What is correct?
options: Leave it in, keep him still and call 911
Push it in further to stop bleeding
Soak the chest in hot water
quiz.why: Removing it can cause serious bleeding. Hospital teams remove it safely.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Stings and bites: bees to spiders
lessons.when: Stung or bitten by a bee, wasp, hornet, ant, scorpion, centipede or spider.
recognize: Pain, redness and swelling at the site; a bee leaves its stinger behind
Large swelling of a whole limb over a day or two is usually a local reaction
Anaphylaxis: trouble breathing, wheeze, throat tightness or hoarse voice
Anaphylaxis: swollen lips, tongue or face, dizziness, fainting, pale floppy child
Hives all over plus vomiting or belly pain can also be anaphylaxis
Scorpion in a child: sweating, vomiting, drooling, restlessness, fast breathing
steps: Watch for anaphylaxis signs. If present, use their adrenaline auto-injector in the outer thigh and call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Move away from the nest or insects; wasps and bees can attack in groups.
Remove a bee stinger as fast as possible by scraping or plucking; speed matters more than method.
Wash the area with soap and water.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for about 10 to 20 minutes to ease pain and swelling.
Raise the limb, and give paracetamol or an antihistamine for itch if they can take them.
Scorpion or centipede: same care, and take young children to a clinic promptly.
Spider bite: wash and cool; seek care if pain is severe, it spreads or they feel unwell.
dont: Do not wait to see if anaphylaxis gets better; give adrenaline early.
Do not give an antihistamine instead of adrenaline in anaphylaxis.
Do not cut or squeeze the sting site.
Do not scratch; it raises the risk of infection.
lessons.call: Call at once for any sign of anaphylaxis, stings in the mouth or throat, or many stings at once. See a doctor for a scorpion sting in a child or a sting that becomes hot, spreading and painful after a day.
special: Children are more at risk from scorpion venom and multiple stings; seek care early.
Anaphylaxis in pregnancy: still give adrenaline and lie her on her left side.
Anyone who has had a severe reaction should see a doctor about carrying adrenaline.
lessons.why: Most stings and bites cause pain and swelling that settle with cooling and time. A bee stinger keeps pumping venom for a short while, so getting it out quickly reduces the dose; the old advice to only scrape it is less important than speed. A big swollen limb on its own is usually a local reaction, not anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is a whole body allergic reaction that can close the airway or drop the blood pressure within minutes. Adrenaline reverses it; antihistamines are too slow and too weak. That is why you act on breathing, throat or fainting signs straight away. In South-East Asia, most scorpion and spider bites are painful but not deadly to adults, though small children can react more strongly.

quiz.q: After a wasp sting, your friend's lips swell and her voice turns hoarse. What first?
options: Use her adrenaline auto-injector in the outer thigh and call 911
quiz.why: Hoarse voice and swollen lips are anaphylaxis. Adrenaline first, then call.

quiz.q: A bee sting leaves the stinger in your arm. What is the key point?
options: Only ever scrape it with a card
Get it out as fast as possible by any method
Leave it in for a doctor
Squeeze the sting to push out venom
quiz.why: Speed of removal matters more than the method.

quiz.q: A day after a sting, the whole forearm is swollen and itchy but he breathes and feels fine. What is this?
options: A large local reaction: cool, raise, antihistamine, see a doctor if spreading pain or fever
quiz.why: Local swelling without body wide signs is not anaphylaxis, but watch for infection.

sources: AHA and American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines (2024 update)

lessons.title: Suicidal thoughts and acute distress
lessons.when: Someone talks about suicide, may harm themselves, or is overwhelmed, panicking or in acute distress.
recognize: Talking about wanting to die, being a burden, or having no reason to live
Looking for ways to kill themselves, such as pills, pesticide, rope or a weapon
Saying goodbye, giving things away, or a sudden calm after deep sadness
Withdrawing, feeling hopeless or trapped, drinking or using drugs more
Panic: racing heart, fast breathing, shaking, fear of dying or losing control
steps: If they are in immediate danger or have already harmed themselves, call emergency services (911 in the Philippines).
Stay with them, or make sure someone safe does. Find a calm, private place.
Ask directly and kindly: Are you thinking about killing yourself? Asking does not put the idea in their head.
Listen without judging or arguing. Say: Thank you for telling me. I am here. We will get help.
Remove or lock away anything they could use: medicines, pesticides, knives, ropes, and keep them away from heights.
Call the NCMH Crisis Hotline with them: 1553 (landline) or 0919-057-1553, 0917-899-8727, 0966-351-4518. Free, 24 hours.
For panic, breathe slowly with them, in through the nose, longer out through the mouth; name things they can see.
Help them make a plan for the next hours: who stays with them, who to call, and a doctor visit.
Check in again later and the next day. Look after yourself too.
dont: Do not promise to keep thoughts of suicide a secret.
Do not lecture, argue, or say things like you have so much to live for.
Do not leave someone at high risk alone, even briefly.
Do not put yourself in danger; if there is a weapon, get away and call 911.
lessons.call: Call 911 if they have a plan and the means, have harmed themselves, taken an overdose or poison, or you cannot keep them safe. Otherwise call the NCMH Crisis Hotline 1553 together, now.
special: Young people may show distress through anger, withdrawal or self harm; take every mention of suicide seriously.
After childbirth, a mother with despair, confusion or thoughts of harming herself or her baby needs urgent care today.
Older people living alone, and people after a recent loss, need regular check ins.
lessons.why: People thinking about suicide often feel alone and unable to see a way out, and the most intense urge usually passes in hours. Your job is to help them through that window and connect them to help. Asking directly about suicide is safe: research shows it brings relief and does not raise the risk. Listening calmly helps them feel less alone. Removing the means is one of the most effective ways to prevent death, because many attempts are impulsive; in rural Asia pesticides are a common method, so lock them away. Crisis lines are staffed by trained counsellors who can guide both of you. Slow breathing with a long out breath calms the body's alarm response in panic.

quiz.q: A friend says she cannot go on and everyone would be better off without her. What should you do?
options: Change the subject to cheer her up
Ask her directly if she is thinking about suicide and listen
Tell her she is being dramatic
quiz.why: Asking directly is safe and opens the door to help.

quiz.q: He tells you he has saved up pills to take tonight. What is the priority?
options: Leave him to sleep on it
Stay with him, remove the pills and call 911 or the 1553 crisis line
Argue about why it is wrong
quiz.why: A plan and means mean high risk. Remove the means, stay, and get help now.

quiz.q: Which is the NCMH Crisis Hotline landline number in the Philippines?
quiz.why: 1553 is the nationwide toll free landline. Mobile: 0919-057-1553, 0917-899-8727 or 0966-351-4518.

sources: WHO Psychological First Aid: Guide for field workers (2011)
National Center for Mental Health (Philippines) Crisis Hotline

lessons.title: Emergency childbirth
lessons.when: A baby is coming before you can reach a hospital or midwife.
recognize: Strong contractions every 2 to 3 minutes or less
A strong urge to push or to open the bowels
Waters breaking, sometimes with a little blood
The baby's head visible at the vaginal opening during a contraction
steps: Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines). Stay on the line; the dispatcher will coach you.
Wash your hands, use gloves if you have them, and lay out clean towels or cloth.
Let her choose a comfortable position, such as half sitting, on her side, or on hands and knees.
Let the baby come by itself and gently support the head; never pull. Ease any cord around the neck over the head.
Hold the baby firmly; newborns are slippery. Put the baby straight onto her bare chest.
Dry the baby well with a towel, then cover both with a dry blanket, including the baby's head.
Not breathing or crying after drying? Keep the head level, give 5 gentle breaths, and follow the dispatcher.
Do not cut the cord. Let the placenta come by itself, keep it beside the baby, and take it to hospital.
After the placenta, firmly rub her lower belly and help the baby breastfeed to reduce bleeding.
dont: Do not pull on the baby or the cord.
Do not try to delay the birth by holding her legs together.
Do not cut the cord unless told to by a professional.
Do not bathe the baby; keep it warm and skin to skin.
lessons.call: Call as soon as labour starts early or fast. Stop and wait for professional help, keeping her calm, if the bottom or feet come first, the cord comes out first, there is heavy bleeding, or the baby is stuck.
special: Cord comes out first: call, get her on her knees with chest down and bottom up, and do not push the cord back.
Premature babies lose heat very fast: skin to skin and cover well, including the head.
Heavy bleeding after birth: keep rubbing her lower belly firmly, keep the baby at the breast, and call again.
lessons.why: Most births happen by themselves, and your role is to keep mother and baby safe, clean and warm until help arrives. Pulling on the baby or cord can injure them, so let contractions do the work. Newborns lose heat fast, and drying them also stimulates breathing, which is why drying and skin to skin contact come first. Most babies breathe on their own within a minute; gentle breaths help the few who do not. There is no rush to cut the cord, and an unsterile cut can cause infection. After the placenta comes out, the womb needs to contract to stop bleeding: rubbing the lower belly and breastfeeding both help. Breech births, a cord coming first or heavy bleeding need professional skills, so get help urgently.

quiz.q: The baby's head is out and the cord is loosely around its neck. What do you do?
options: Gently slip the cord over the head and let the birth continue
quiz.why: A loose cord can usually be eased over the head. Never pull the baby.

quiz.q: The baby is born. What comes first?
options: Dry the baby and place it skin to skin on the mother, covered
quiz.why: Drying keeps the baby warm and stimulates breathing. Skin to skin keeps it warm.

quiz.q: During labour, the cord appears before the baby. What do you do?
options: Call 911, put her on knees with chest down and bottom up, wait for help
quiz.why: This position takes pressure off the cord. It is an emergency needing professional help.

sources: ERC Guidelines 2021: Newborn resuscitation and support of transition
